NOTICE IS HEREBY 3IVEN, that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace to rthe COUNTY OF CHESTER will be holden at the CASTLE OF CHESTER, in and for the said Ci;unty, on MONDAY, the 2nd day of July, 1906, at half-ppst E'even o'clock in the forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing ot all Appeals arising within the Hundreds ofißroxton,Eddisbury, Nantwich, and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from suchlluadreds will take place at sueh Sessions. The Grand and Petty Juries for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of the court on MONDAY, the 2nd day of July, 1906, at half-past Eleven o'clock in Forenoon, _ _ . _

THE Court will be adjourned to the Court HOU6P, Knutsford, on WEDNESDAY, the 4th day of July, 1906, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenocin,when another Grand Jury will be empannelled. The bearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Bucklow, Macclesfield. and Northwicb, forming the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last- mentioned Hundreds will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Petty Juries for the Knutsford District must be in attendance at the Court Rousel Knutaford, at the opening of the Court OD WEDNESDAY, the 4th day of July, 1906, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon.
REGINALD POTTS. Clerk of the Peace for the C)unty of Cbester. Chester, 13t4 June, 1908.

Wills sent over for Blundell in 1 the afternoon, and spoke to him kindly, ba with firmness. "Perhaps I may say, Captain Blundell, that the Commander-in-Chief is rather hasty. And I can I assure you, unless you clear yourself pretty otis. I factorily, he will certainly revise his opinion. Personally, I trust you will discover the person who is responsible,. and get him—or her=to come forward. 7 And that certainly did not cheer Dick Blundell. Sooner than disgrace Madge, he would quit the Service, though it broke his heart. Ile left for Bombay that night after writing a private letter to Colonel Briggs, in which he told him something of whak had occurred. He wrote to Billy too, just a line to say he was going home on private affairs. To Gwynne he sent a note, and requested tun to give his love to the little Goorkhas, for whom he prayed that Sri Ganga mother might give them rivers of blood to swim in, and many enemies to cut up. And somehow it leaked out that Blundell was More or less in disgrace, and after all might get no recognition in the anxiously-expected honours for the Gulistan Relief Force. On hearing this, Billy, who now swore to Ilundell, wrote home a most indignant letter to Madge, and in his best "I say, come now, by Jove!" style, raved for four whole pages. It followed Bhindell in the next steamer, and was only a week behind him. . But as Blundell crossed the black water, 'be was inore and more in an evil case, and saw nu way . out of the trouble. , Glad though lie might be that Sir Eustace Cam- borne was obviously no friend of Sir Dan, yet little Wills's dry caution stuck in his mind. Could he even see Vadge ? And if he saw her, what could he say? To let her know that her effort to help him had ruined him would be asking her to cbnfess her plot openly. He could not do it. _ Put if he•was unable to do that he could at any rate have it out with the Adjutant-General, and he promised himself some compensation for long years of bitterness. What a fool he had been, though, to have ever competed for the favour of a Madam Fly-by-Night (for such she was in essence) with '.a man wile held his future in his bands. There had been suppressed, and, indeed, unsappressed laughter about Sir Dan when the fortune of the day went avainst the General Commanding, and the voune Hussar subaltern carried off the nrize. But before he made up his mind what to do, Madge had received Billy's letter from India, and was in a most terrible state of mind, (To hie enntinus€Ll 01'

BAPTIST SUNDAY SCHOOL TRENT.—Tho annual Sun- day school treat in connection with Hill Cliffe Baptist Church was held on Monday, the children being taken by lurries and a 'bus to Walnut Tree Farm (Mr.Kinsefs) Stretton. The clagnbeing fine there was a good muster, seven lurries and alnus,with the conveyances of friends, being requisitioned. The farm was reathed about one o'clock, where Mr. Kinsey had made capital provision for the entertainment of all, swinzs,see-saw, &c., having been erected in a field. After giving the children buns and milk, they played to their hearts' content until four o'clock, when tea was provided in the great iron shed, and was much enjoyed. Afterwards races were indulged in by the various classes, and prizes given. The usual games followed, until 8.30 p.m., when there was a rally at the house. " All hail the power" was sung. The Pastor (the Rev. J. S. Hughes) spoke a few words an the enjoyment of the day and the great kind- ness of Mr. Kinsey and family and Mr. Joseph Mross, jun.. the superintendent, proposed a vote of thanks, which was seconded by Mr. E. L. Jones, supported by Mr. Deakin, and passed with three cheers for all the family. The visitors started for home at nine o'clock, and reached Hill Cliffe at ten.

LIGHTNING FLASHES EXTRAORDINARY.

A 41n. black disc, marked with a white cross, and rotated fifty to sixty times a second, has - been used by a German at night for studying lightning flashes. Some flashes caused the cross to appear once, others brought it out several times, and repeated observations confirmed the view that the discharge is very variable. The duration of some seemed to be aLcut I,oooth part of a second. Others were shorter, and some were evidently not snore than a 35,000 th part of a second. Faraday thought flashes were at least • one second longer.

How Ila Huta Hrmsum—The tramp is a student of human nature, at least that human nature which is feminine, and which has its little jealousies over the dockyard fence. He knows what neighbour women think of each other, and he turns it to the best accoun in his favour. Such a tramp came to the kitchen door of a house in Third-street, Chicago, the other day, and he was assisted in his walk by a crutch. The lady,of the mansion happened to open the door for him. "My," she exclaimed at first sight, "what's the matter ?" "I'm hungry, ma'am," he replied. "That isn't why you are wearing a crutch, is it?" "No, ma'am," he smiled, "I hurt myself yesterday." "How did you do it?" Ile looked nervously over towards the adjoining house, and lowered his voice. " I hope I ain't doin' wrong, ma'am, tellin" he said, "but the lady next door gave me a loaf of bread of her own mak in', she said, and I drapped it on my foot and it crippled me, ma'am." "Oh," chuckled the lady, and with is generous spirit she brought him the best in her larder. ,

RELATIVE VALUES.—One day stopping at a house for dinner in the Kentucky mountains I listened to an agent trying to sell the head of the establishment' a sewing machine. "Now, look here," said the agent, " you ought to do something to help your wife, oughtn't you? " She ain't objectin' to my style, I reckon," said the rnountaineet. "That's because he a good, kind, uncomplaining sort of a woman, and it is the very reason why you should do these little things for her." "But I can't afford it," pro- tested the mountaineer. "Afford it, nothing," ex- claimed the agent. "You could afford to buy that Winchester sitting by the door couldn't you ?" The mountaineer 'looked up quickly and reached for the gun. " Yes," he said, lay- ing it across his lap, " but I needed it." "Not as much as your wife needs a sewing machine." "More, I reckon." "Of .course that isn't so. How could you? Now rthll you what I'll do. If you will buy a machine for your wife I'll take the gun as part pay." "I reckon not." "Call your wife out here and ask her what she thinks about it. I'll .bet a hat she'll jump at the chance for such at exchange. The mountaineer, smiled and called thc "old Aroman" out. He stated the proposition to het and the agent began to feel sure of victory. "If Jim Bolton wasn't livin' we might," she said after e moment's thought. "What's he got to do with it?' asked the agent in a provoked tone. "A heap sight You see," she went on, "my old man an'4im ain't or terms; that's why he got the Winchester. Now el Jim , knowed we only had a sewin' machine, it wouldn't be no time till I wuz a widder, an' I reckon I'll do my sewin' by hand. S'pose you come round after Jim's fixed,' and the agent gave it up anc agreed to come around after James had been dis. posed of.

div.head: CAUSE OF WHITE HAIR.
div.p: CAUSE OF WHITE HAIR.

One of the explanations for the hair turnia7 white is that the individual hairs become dry with age, and that the ail penetrating into their interior destroys their colouring matter. Oth-2rs have said that the colouring matter of the I sir of any part of the body disappears under the in. fluence of a chemical substance. Aocoraing to Dr. Metchnikoff, however, hair is not an Melt material; it is alive, and is composed of living cells provided with prolongations which envelcla and destroy colouring Substances in contact wall them. These cells in this way, we are told in a Lancet report, gradually destro7 the colouring matter of the hair, and spread in each direction both towards the root of the hair and tomirds its extremity. This may be recognised by. the fact that after the greater portion of the hair has to- come white the root still remains coloured.

div.head: MOSQUITO-EATING FISH:
div.p: MOSQUITO-EATING FISH:

The importance of the mosquito in spread- ing malarial diseases is fully recognised. Hence the study of its natural enemies is also of special interest. In the Barbadoes many of the waters abouhd in a small fish known as "millions"— presumably from their great numbers—which feeds on the lame of the mosquito. It is said that in the parts where the fish abounds there is immunity from mosquitoes, and that malaria is almost unknown. Experiments are to be tried by introducing the fish into other islands of the West Indies. This plan of introducing a natural enemy has proved successful in a number of cases, and the mosquito-eating fish might be introduced into other. districts. If this fish really feeds largely on the larva of the mosquito, and if the latter have really become extinct in the district, we have the unusual case of species ex- terminating its own food supply.

div.head: HYDROGEN FOR BALLOONS.
div.p: HYDROGEN FOR BALLOONS.

------- -- A new method of preparing hydrogen, which should be of advantage in Ellin:7; lialit.cmi 'kr military purposes, has been explained to the French Academy by Professor Moissa.n. The material used is a new chemical compound dis- covered by M. Joubert, and said to be a sort of hydrate of calcium. It is prepared by the action of metallic calcium on some metallic salt, and its' commercial name is "hydrolithe," that is, water. stone. When water is added, hydrogen is copi- ously evolved, 11b. of the pure salt yielding 14 onbio feet of gas, and lib. of the commercial article rather more than 16 cubic feet., The smaller quantity of the material required to yield a given amount of gas constitutes the great , advantage of "hydrolithe" over the usual zino and sulphuric acid. For while to fill a field bal- loon of 17,657 cubic feet capacity some three tons ' of the latter, requiring three ..waggons and six ' horses for its carnage, are needed, one ton of hydrolithe, which can be conveyed in one two- I horse waggon, will supply the same amount of gas.

div.head: HOW SNAILS SMELL.
div.p: HOW SNAILS SMELL.

In many animals the sense of smell attains a high degree of perfection, and serves an im- portantpurpose. Professor Emil Yung, of the! University of Geneva, has been experimenting ! with snails with a view of locating the olfactory ; organs. The species experimented on was ; Helix pommatia. The snail was known to have • a strong sense of smell, but it was not known in ' what part of the body this sense was located. Professor Yung's experiments seem to show that.. the snail smells with all parts of its body not coverqd by the shell, but that the mott highly sensitive parts are the two pairs of tentacles, the lips, and the edges of the foot. • When a -brush ; wetted with a drop of water was brought to- wards the snail, no effect was produced until it actually touched it, except in the case of ; the large tentacles containing the eyes. ! These were perceptibly affected at a dis- tance of one millimetre. This, Professor ! Yung considers, was not due to sight or the sense of heat, but to smell. When camo- mile essence was used instead of water, tho odour I was perceived at a distance of four millimetres, and this was shewn by a deflection of the ten- . taeles. In a similar way, the essence of camo- mile caused depression of the back, and turning . of the edge of the foot at the same distance.. When the experiments were repeated, the re-! sponse on the part of the snail 'became less marked. Professor Yung concludes that smell ' plays quite a secondary part in the sail's quest for food.

div.head: SAFE-BREAKING BY ELECTRICITY.
div.p: SAFE-BREAKING BY ELECTRICITY.

The most recent development in the burglar's profession, says Science Siftings, is the use of electricity to open safes in place of the old-time jimmy and the more recent dynamite. An ex- pert burglar, who has " retired from business after amassing a sufficient competency," has de- , monstrated that by the aid of electricity he : could within a short time reduce safes of the . highest repute to old iron. For this purpose he took out of his pocket a style in the form of re- , tort carbon, similar to those used for arc lamps,! a few yards of electric wire, black +glasses, and a plate pierced in the middle. It was with ' this simple outfit he pierced in less than three minutes a circle of holes in a cast steel safe with • walls one and a-half inches thick. His method of oprsocupedpluy nt i the simplicity procedure was sili itself. To the °lee- chandelier overhead he I connected two wires, one of which he fixed on wrreonp the safe and the other at the extreme of his ear- bon style. It was suitably insulated by a wooden handle. Then, half inserting this pencil in the hole of the plate, whose purpose was to protect , him against the heat and light, he produced a I voltaic arc of immense power between the point. of his style and the wall of the safe, thus mete lug the metal with the greatest ease. , I AT THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA.

Cold, darkness, and monotony—such are the characteristic features of the ocean bed, says a writer in the Scientiiie American. The compo- sition of the floor itself is the only thing that ! changes, though this is only the case close to the coast, as no alteration (or very little) seems . to occur at great depths. Investigations made with drags, dredgers, sounding apparatus, and the like, have shewn that it is an error to assume that the bed of the ocean is covered with sand, as this latter is essentially a coast formation only found in comparatively shallow water, close to . the shore. Mud begins to take its place the further we go afield—mud, or rather, ooze. Its origin varies considerably; a part consis,ts of the alluvial deposits brought down by rivdrs. This ooze is of various kinds. Blue ooze is found close to schistous coasts, and its hue is imparted to it by organic substances and iron pyrites; it covers the floor of the Mediterranean and of the Arctic Ocean. Red 'ooze is merely the blue ' variety changed in colour by the peroxidation of the iron; it is also formed of the - - - ALLUVIAL DEPOSITS -

brought down by rivers flowing through land i rich n iron, such, for instance, as the Cpngo and some rivers in Brazil. Green ooze, finally, owes its colour to glauconite; it is found along • rocky coasts where there are no rivers. In many places the sand or ooze is mixed with volcanic elements originating from terrestrial and submarine explosions. The inorganic world, ; hhwever, is not the only source from which the ocean bed receives its supplies of material. The remains of organic creatures also oontribute no , mean share. The upper strata of the sea swarm with teeming animal life—alga, crustacea, eggs, larva. &c.—of all kinds, which die daily• in thousands and slowly sink downward to the lowest depths of the sea, thus forming a CONTINUAL RAIN OF ooursES of tdgS, diatoms, et hoc genus omne Which descend from heights far exceeding those of Mount Everest (33.755 ft. and other lofty terres- I t trial peaks. Protozoidal forms, foraminifers and ' radiolarite (over 1.000,000 of which would not , weigh an ounce, but which are so fertile that 1 one specimen can produce 70,000,000 direct and indirect descendants in four days) also play a ' highly important part in this work. Due to their shells, the foraminifera form large quanti- ties of calcareous deposits. The .globigerinie members of this family) form a which is found in e bed of the specialAanlan e nheile the the radiolarise form silicious de- I posits which abound in the Pacific and Indian Oceans, where a SPECIAL KIND OF OOZE

is also found, viz., the pteropod—Ooze composed'. of the shells of pteropod mollusks which is found at the bottom of the Atlantic between Africa and America and near tho Azores. These oozes. however, are not permanent, but merely re- present a phase or stage. died, blue, and brown clay is the only permanent compound ; it is soft, aroasy to tho touch l and contains from 1 to 20 per cent, or lime, a lime vitrinanie earth, and , organic remains. The oozes referred to above gradually torn into red clay, which thus becomes the final tomb of all that has lived. mov9dl and . , had its biro a• toe sea.

div.head: BOILS AND ABSCESSES.

Seasonable Shia Disorders Which Yield to Zam-Buk.

div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.

The usual meeting was held on Sunday afternoon last, when Mr. G. Smiley, in the absence of the speaker, presided, and also gave the address. He spoke upon Sowing and its importance." Attention to good seed, he said, brought its blessings and harvest ; but the sowing of bad seed or tares brought its own harvest of failure.—Mr. Taylor and Mr. A. Healey took part in the meeting. Mr. W. H. Payton' Mus. Bac.,presided.at the organ and rendered a solo in his usual able style. The Secretary announced that 21125. Bd. had been received that day towards the fund for repairing the organ.—The Secretary moved a vote of sympathy with. Mr. Hilton, whose premises had been greatly damaged with fire the night before.

Christian Endeavour Rally. The annual"rally and echo meeting"in conection with the Warrington and District Union of Christian Endeavour Societies was held on Saturday at Hill Cliffe. In the. afternoon about 40 young people met and, guided by the Rev. J. S. Hughes, had a delightful ramble along the lanes, and through the fields, returning to partake of tea in the schoolroom at five o'clock, when a larger company met. After tea there was a meeting in the schoolroom for the purpose of hearing "Echoes " of the great convention in Leeds. Mr. W. T. Moss, of I Tom (president of the society) took the chsir, and interest- ing addresses were given by the Misses Mason and Siddall and Mr. Moss, Solos were also rendered by friends.

div.head: Rev. H. Dannlce at Liverpool.
div.p: Rev. H. Dannlce at Liverpool.

We extract, the following from the" Liverpool Daily Post. and Mercuri, " :—At Kensington Baptist Church on Sunday special sermons were delivered in connection with the Sunday School Anniversary by the Rev. Herbert Donnie° (the minister-elect of/ this church). I Owing to the inclemency of the weather the morning service was not as largely attended as it would have been, but the evening compensated for this, as the church has rarely been so crowded, an&no doubt most 'present came to hear the new minister. Mr. Dunnico preached on the "New Birth," and it was delightful to hear such broad views, full of charity to every section of the Christian Church and full of hope to humanity in its most depraved state. Althilugh scathing in his denunciation of those who narrowed down the Gospel to their own little creed, he rejoiced in his belief that in every man's heart there was a latent Christ which would break forth into newness of life when it res- ponded to the Christ of God or the outward Christ. There was a true ring of sincerity in every word of the preacher,(and no doubt when Mr. Dunnico settles in this church he wilßbe a great power for good in this city, and the officers and members have been wise in their selection of such a minister. Mr. Richardson spoke at the flower service in the afternoon, which was conducted by Mr. Oxford (the superintendent). Alto- gether the services were most successful. •

div.head: Hill Cliffe Summer Sermons.
div.p: Hill Cliffe Summer Sermons.

The summer services in connection with Hill Cliffe Baptist Church which were held on Sunday were, on the whole, well attended. In the morning the rain descended heavily, and there was consequently not so arge an attendance of children at the flower service as usual. The Pastor presided and the Rev. Dr. Witton Davies, of Bangor University, gave an interesting address on " The flowers of Palestine," illustrated by a quantity of the actual flowers collected by him during his travels in Palestine. In the afternoon, the weather having partly cleared, there was a good attend- ance. The doctor again preached, taking as his text the words "I will go with thee and lo I am with thee unto the end of the world." He showed how God had been with men in the performance of their mission in life. Miss Patti-May Roberts, of Liverpool, sang with great effect "A voice that bids me come" and "But the Lord is mindful of His own." In the evening the, chapel was crowded. The pulpit was again occupied byl Mr. Davies, who preached upon the words" How shall we escape if we neglect so great salvation ? " treating the subject from a new standpoint, the standpoint of the higher critics,with whom the doctor is in sympathy, and is engaged now in preparing one of the volumes of the twentieth Century Bill. Miss Roberts sang "Abide with me" and " Jesu, lover of my soul" most effec- tively. The choir also tendered the anthem "Therefore with the angels," very well. The organists for the day were Mr. James Strange and Mr. Willie Hallas, Mrs. Hughes being the accompanist. The collections amounted to almost £2O.

div.head: Warrington Independent Methodists and Incorporation Proposals.
div.p: Warrington Independent Methodists and Incorporation Proposals.

At the 101st Independent Methodist conference held at Roe Green, Worsley, on Tuesday the question of incorporation was introduced in a motion by Mr. W. Price, of Wigan, deeming it expedient to proceed forth- with to register the memorandum and articles of asso- ciation. He claimed that the time was now ripe for ' placing their connexions' funds upon the only safe and sound basis which incorporation provided, and really give effect to the standing resolutions of the Con- nexion.—Mr. Bartle (Sunderland) seconded the resolu- tion.—Mr. R. Henshall (Warrington) asked for a post- ponement of the matter for twelve months, in order that a round table conference might be held, with the object of arriving at a common basis of union. He feared there would be churches who could no longer associate themselves with the denomina- tion if incorporation were adopted. He hoped such a crisis as was threatened would be avoided.— Mr. Dodd (Liverpool) seconded.— Mr. Dale (Warrington), said the church which he represented at Friars Green, Warrington, was the foundation church of Independent Methodism, and they had decided to vote against incorporation, even to the point of splitting up.'—The President hoped no threats or intimidation would be indulged in by delegate.—Mr. W. Brimelow (Bolton) said it was the opinion of eminent counsel that a voluntary elected annual meet- ing could not have any control over an incorporated association as proposed. He was introduced to Con- nexional service at the previous annual assembly held at Roe Green in 1866, and it was pathetic that the link after forty years' service might be broken at the same place.—The voting was taken by ballot and declared as follows :—For the amendment, 34 ; against, 113. The resolution was afterwards adopted on the under- standing that the position should be reviewed five years hence.

div.head: Rev. John Yonge and Women's Rights. The Conduct of the Suffragettes.
div.p: Rev. John Yonge and Women's Rights. The Conduct of the Suffragettes.

At Wycliffe Church on Sunday evening the Rev John Yong° based his sermon on the words: There cometh a woman of Samaria to draw water. Jesus saith unto her, give me to drink. . . His disciples marvelled that He talked with the woman "(John iv.. 7 and 27). He said the incident described in the text helped to remind them that in their very midst that night Jesus came to women with a personal request for sympathy and service. To the woman of Samaria herself and to the disciples the condescension and friendliness of the master's conduct to s woman was the occasion of irrepressible marvel. The way of the ancient world with woman was that of ever keeping her in a rank inferior to man. It was not insensible of her frequent and characteristic beauty. Nor was it alto- gether unresponsive to the influence and charm of her tenderness and love. Nor, again, was it unconscious of the value and even preciousness of her self-forgetful service. But at best it always thought of her in a way in which even the Christian Apostle allowed himself to describe her as" the weaker vessel." That was a phrase, surely, which no woman at any rate would regard as being verbally inspired. It was not until Jesus came— "made of a woman "—that woman rose to her full dignity and came towards her true position of equality in the human family. He (the preacher) supposed there would always be mean. ungenerous, and cowardly men who would attribute all the evils of human nature to the frailty of Eve in the garden of Eden. But it should

bring such mean imputations to an end when they recol- lected that when Mary became the mother of the I World's Saviour woman did all that woman could for r the salvation and welfare of the race. Wherever Christianity had gone it had uplifted womanhood. From 1 being man's serf and Ave, it had raised her to become man's friend and equal. And the more Christian the. world got to be, the better would it be for woman. Woman's real rights would become more recognized I and respected as the spirit of Christ pervaded I' society. The 7 were yet very considerably unrealized, I even in the most Christian lands Even yet woman was made by statute law to feel her legal and I social inferiority. Still was she deemed incapable of exercising political power as the man could'do. ,The I most illiterate and immoral and evil man had more power than the best and wisest and most accomplished woman. I She was kept outside. the franchise. She was still dis- qualified for the profession of law. She fright not take part in municipal work. She was not deemed deserving I of equal wage with men for work and service. She , might indeed work longer hours for less pay than a man I whose hours were less. She was "sweated" , mercilessly even by her own sex who would buy " cheap " goods because they were cheap! although they knew ihat their pockets were I being saved at the sacrifice of the health, comfort, j happiness, and legitimate profit of their sisters. There I were manifold and painful and shameful penalties for having been born a woman. That was a terrible and 1 humiliating truth, even yet. And while it ought to I make men's faces burn with shame, it ought to blanch women's faces with pain and grief. He supposed that I very few of his hearers could read recent accounts of violent public disorder on the part of women , in their attempts to secure what were teclmi- I cally known as "Women's rights," without regret I and even censure. But they ought to be fair and candid enough to admit that the public indifference to the social and political claims of women had been so long continued and so stolid and obstinate that the bold resoluteness of women in asserting their claims might be forgiven for sometimes passing the limits of patience and moderation. He supposed they believed—at any rate, he did—that the historic efforts of enslaved people to arrive at freedom had been and I Still were prompted from above, and not from beneath. I "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is, and I there comes liberty." And hence be believed that to-day, in the appeal of " sweated" women who cried out against the greed and tyranny of their task-masters, and in the demand of intel- ligent womanhood to have share in the national Government for which they were compelled to pay, the Spirit of the Lord and Saviour of womanhood was to be recognized. Ever since Jesus met the Samaritan woman at the well, %manhood had been advancing to , her true position, her freedom, and her rights. The more Jesus Christ was believed in and obeyed, the more would woman come to her own. And when she did so, when equality before the law and equality in social and commercial value, and equality of every kind came to be woman's birthright, the wonder would be, not that she had attained it, but that ever she was denied it.

div.head: St. Barnabas' Church.
div.p: St. Barnabas' Church.

The services in celebration of the patronal festival were continued on Sunday and were well attended. At the choral celebration of the Holy Communion in the morning the Vicar(Rev.J.H. G. Hollingworth) preached. As the offertories were on behalf of the Day and Sun- day school funds he devoted his sermon to the educa- tion question, contending that Churchpeople had no" objection to Bible teaching if they were allowed to tench the whole of the Bible in the schools. What they objected to was a mutilated Bible. He proceeded to criticise the various provisions of the Bill which he considered ought to meet with the opposition of all earnest Churchpeople.—At Evensong the preacher was the Rev. H. A. fsester who spoke at some lngth on the importance of definite religious instruction in the schools. He said he felt sure that if the vast iass of people in this land could only be got to realize how momentous was the issue at stake in the struggle which was going on around the schools they would leave no stone unturned to see that the sacrifices made by their forefathers in the cause of Christian education bad not been made in vain. Every- one who thought about education at all must agree that the most important part of it, indeed the great aim and end of all eaucation,was not merely intellectual results, but the formation of character. Neither from the indi- vidual nor theiseeial point of view was it a gain to develop in a 'child keen intellect and a retentive memory unless they taught that child to be honest, industrious, self-controlled and dependable. He maintained without hesitation that it was impossible to train the highest character xvitliont a definite religions basis. If as a nation we lost our religious beliefs and rejected our religious sanctions our stwkard of moral conduct would soon fall and the nation stolid rush headlong to ruin and decay. Religious education, he held, should not be regarded as a mere "extra " but should he a definite and vital part of every day's work, given by teachers trained in the principles of the Church, whom they could trust, who were ken ia to teach the faith that was n them, and of whose faith and life there was some guarantee of fitness. Churchpeople were contending in this matter for the barest justice ; they wanted no privilege or favour.

div.head: " Criticism and Life."
div.p: " Criticism and Life."

There was an excellent attendance at the meeting of the Fenketh Wesleyan Bible Class on Sunday, Mr. C. E. Parker, president, occupying the chair. An address was delivered by the Rev. J. F. Matthews on "Criticism and Life." He desired, he said, at the outfit to dis- tinguish between criticism and fault-finding. Those who found fault seldom found anything else. Those who found fault with all that others did and alleged they could a. so much better themselves usually ended by doing nothing at all. Criticism pure and simple was another thing altogether. It was an art which could be pushed to the last degree of refinement and the faculty should be exercised carefully on a truly scientific basis. Subjective criticism revealed the latent Inclinations and tendencies of the critic's mind and was not always a safe standard of judgment. Objective criticism was equally in error by excluding imagination altogether. It however had the merit of being strictly true to facts and deductions made therefrpm. but the tritest criticism should be a happy blend of the two. Criticism was necessarily destructive but only in so far as it was com- pelled to clear away the rubbish in order to secure a firmer foundation. True criticism, however, was in the end constructive. Its objective was literature and life and the inlinite gradations between the two. In it one might almost say that the whole content of human knowledge became matter for serious scientific investigation. In relation to literature, of the Bible criticism took two forms. There was what was called textual criticism which sought to construct an ideal text, and what was known as the higher criticism, of which many people were unfortunately afraid, and which was an attempt to determine the origin, date and history most only of the various books of the Bible but also of the component parts thereof, if such there were, and determine their relative values to the Bible student. Was there any thing to fear from the higher criticism ? It bad saved many a man's intellect and made the Bible a new thing to those who had been taught to accept every syllable down to the minutest stop as equally valuable and authoritative. •In relation to life criticism sought to point out its best if not its final form, to discover its true basis and exposed for immitation its noblest ideals and received its most fitting expression in the life,spirit and ethics of Jesus Christ.

When Mr. ASQUITH was "THE TRUTH, able to make himself heard AND NOTHING above the screams of BUT---" frantic women the other night, he made some ex- ceedingly just observations concerning the kind of agitation which is being kept up by the clerical opponents of the Education Bill. Misrepresenta- tion, he said, had been reiterated through all the Rural Deaneries of England and Wales. Re added that he had never known misconceptions more perverse, or appeals to passion and prejudice more reckless,than those which have been put for- ward by the opponents and critics of the measure now before this House of Commons. When Mr. ASQUITH reads the speeches of certain Church dignitaries, he rubs his eyes and wonders whether he is living among hobgoblins and chimeras. So do most of us under the same cir- cumstances. If the Education Bill were honestly represented by its opponents there would be an end to agitation at once. The common effort would then be to make it a measure entirely worthy of its excellent intentions. But that may not be when high ecclesiastical personages are leaders in the fray. It is their habit, as Mr. AsQUITH says,to raiso the temperature of a controversy without heightening its tone. They continue to voci- ferate hard words which have no relation to the matter in hand. The other day, in the i House of Commons, Churchmen and Roman Catholics were imploring, the Government to make . it mandatory on the local\ authorities to take over schools offered to them by the denominationalists. They were afraid, that is to say, that in many instances their schools would, not be taken over. And yet we hear talk of confiscation. It may be well to give an instance of what confiscation means under the Bill. A London school-manager, who / also happens to be the headmaster of a Church ' school,was explaining that he would have preferred to see matters work themselves out under Mr. BALFOUR'S measure ; but that he had no objection to Mr. BIRRELL'S bill, which would be distinctly beneficial to a school which be conducted for a period of fifteen yea"'

The owners of the fabric would get £lOO a year for rent. They would save 60 a year On wear and tear, they would have the use of the schools for their own special purposes, and the children would be taught the catechism twice a-week where it has hitherto been taught only once a-week. That is a fairly' typical instance of What is likely to take place under the Bill. What relation has this to anything which, by the furthest stretch of language, can be called cone bscation? Or, to take another variety of those per- versions of truth of which Mr. Asomrn com- plains, what possible justificatien can there be either for describing the religions instruction to be given under the Bill as Nonconformist religion, Or sneering at it as County Council religion? What will be taught is equally the religion of Nonconformity and of the Church of England. There is nothing specially Nonconformist in the Lord's Prayer or the Ten Commandments. The Apostles',Creed is not Nonconformist. The Bible, said STILLINGFLEET, is the religion of Protestants There tit'e many elergymen of the Church of England to whom the word Protes'antism, and all that took place at the Reformation, is hateful; but the bulk of Churchmen, we take leave to believe, are not willing to wholly surrender the Bible to Nonconformity. In the schools, besides what we ilfave indicated, there will he some singing ~h3aems which are in use by almost all sects of "iriatians, and there will be some simple prayers. SurelY that is enough for children, the bulk of t horn are brought under other religious influences a the home or in the Sunday-school. It has been adjudged to be enough by very high authorities in the Established Church when there was no educa- tional controversy to the fore. It would be con- sidered to be enough now by all men who are not I extremists in these matters if there were not before the House of Commons a measure designed to put the national system of education on a more just basis than it has ever before occupied, and in a condition of efficiency from which it has been debarred by religious differences.

The Warrington Free FREE Cuunca Church Council is to be Acrivrnr. congratulated on its Chris- tian enterpi ise and the iacrifice of its members. A series of open-air services is to be given on Sunday evenings in l'arious public places. The best preachers available ;will he secured, and the singing will be led by a Quid as often as possible. Sunday evening will Beo the first of these services held on the Fair ground to be followed in successive weeks by gatherings at Bewsey-road, Corporation -street, ,14atchford, Stockton Heath, Penketh, and Sankey liridgesAs soon as it can be arranged we hope the ree Church Council will visit the poorer quarters of the town where there is little Sabbath observance

4,nd only a dim knowledge of Christianity. nwick-road, Orford-lane, and Church-street (or tiowley) would be good centres for evangelistic 'work. In comparison, Latchford, Stockton Heath, Penketh have piety enough. The movement ls an admirable one and capable of being made the llleans of doing much real good. We hope it will °e a success in every respect.

Sensible women everywhere are wrathful at the unbridled lawlessness of the savage sufirag- i7tes, who are sufficiently well educated to know better. The thirty years' silent revolution of which Mr. Balfour spoke has not been without its marvellous result. Wears hearing rather much THE REALM OF iN this day about John MIRACLES. Wesley. His" Journal "has been published for a modest silver coin ; so has Southey' Life, and a useful modern Life, besides, while Dr. Fitchett's work on "Wesley and His Century" is now out in volume form. Wesley's history stands for one of the most impressive facts in human experience: " Religion," Newman says in his "Grammar of Assent," is "a system ; it is a rite, a creed, a philosophy, a rule of duty." In the "Grammar of Assent," Dr. Fitchett declares,"is an indefinable note of weariness." Wear- iness is the last thing one would associate with- Wesley. His industry is amazing. Says a well-known entry in his Journal : "I iiave entered into the eighty-third year of my age. I am a wonder to myself. lam never tired, either with preaching, writing, or traveliing." He closed in his ninetieth year a marvellous career as an itinerant preacher of no less a period than fifty-one years. But his life is significant to the modern observer because, "emptied of selfishness," he became the vehicle of so amazing a vitality and power, and the director of so widespread, penetrat in, and subtle a m we'nent. His life was the painful round of a medireval ascetic until he met the Moravians ; then, like a contrary miracle to the smiting of the fig-tree, it became suddenly transfigured, so that Alexander Knox could "dwell with astonished admiration on his unclouded cheerfulness." This change is one of the profound things of psychology. There is little wonder that it draws thinking men no less than does that mysterious Revival of the eighteenth century which was its stupendous national accom- paniment.
Of all the smoker's outfit THE MEERSCHAUM there is nothing that so

PIPE. . - bespeaks devotion to my Lady Nicotine as the meerschaum. The clay pipe is of the lower order for the weary husbandnoan ; the briar is the solace of another order of workers, to be taken out when a knotty point crops up requiring thought, or after a long day's toil. But the meerschanrn is the aristocrat. It is guarded jealowsly in its case; its rising colour is watched with pride and satisfac- tion; it is produced on high-clays and holidays, and its beauties are discussed by the admiring circle. But how many smokers of meerschaums think where 1 the material comes from ? It is "sea foam," they know, but they seldom look further than that. An 1 interesting account of the meerscloaum industry 1 appears in a Brussels journal. Tne district of Eski Shebr in Asia Minor supplies practically the ' whole of the meerschaum consumed throughout the world. Four thousand Kurds and Persians are employed in its production, and the meer- schaum is found in beds of red clay. From the mines it is taken to Eski Shehr, and there cleansed and made ready for the market. Its pro- gress through the stages of preparation is suffi- ciently dignified for so respectable an article. There is an air of aristocracy even about the name of the four classes of quality into which the material is in the last stage assorted : Sviamaly, Birimbirlik, Pernbeli, and Dockum.

DROWNING FATALITY AT LATCHFORD. , Sailor Falls Into Ship Canal. A distressing fatality occurred near Latchford Swing Bridge on Thursday evening. The steamship 1" Sarah Blanche," belonging to the Isle of Man Steam Packet Company, bad passed through the locks, and was passing down the Canal when Joseph Joughin (19), an ordinary seaman, who was washing the deck, fell overboard. He was a good swimmer, but as the vessel was in motion he was drawn under the water and sank immediately. Dragging operations were at once commenced, and after about an hour's work the body was recovered and placed on the " Sarah Blanche " and conveyed to the Isle of Man, where the deceased lived.

div.head: ALDERMANIC VACANCY.
div.p: THE ALDERMANIC VACANCY.

The first business at the July Council meeting will be the election of an alderman to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Alderman John Roberts. If the seniority rule is observed,the honour should be conferred upon a Liberal as the three senior Councillors are all members of the party, Councillors Ellison and Duncan each having served from 1895 while Councillor Burton entered the Council in 189 G. It will be remembered that on the occasion of the last aldermanic election Councillor Ellison was a candidate, but although he had the claim in point of seniority he was defeated by the late Alderman Roberts. It is rumoured that the Con- servatives intend to bring forward either Councillor Forshaw or Councillor Fulton Smith for the seat. Councillor Forshaw has been a member of the Council since 1000, Councillor Fulton Simth being elected in 1904. The Non-Traders have not yet decided upon any definite course of action rind their votes will be an important factor in deciding the election.

div.head: LIBERALS AT BELLE VUE.
div.p: LIBERALS AT BELLE VUE.
30,000 Politicians To Attend To-Morrow's Demonstration.

The visit of Mr. John Burns to Manchester this Saturday, when in company with Mr. Lloyd George and Mr. Winston Churchill, he speaks at a huge Libel al demonstration at Belle Vue, is to be seized upon by the unemployed as a suitable opportunity for extracting from the right hon. gentleman some state- ment as to the intentions of the Government in the direction of further legislation. Permission is being sought for facilities for sending a deputation of the out-o'-works to Mr. Burns. If granted, the right hon. gentleman's reply will be communicated to a meeting of the unemployed to be held outside the garden gates : if it is refused the unemployed will hold an opposition demonstration of their own. Meanwhile arrangements for the Liberal gathering are being completed. It promises to be one of the biggest events of its kind that Manchester has ever known. Lord Stanley of Alderley and a score of local and district members of Parliament are expected to be present, and the crowd, to be recruited from all parts of Lancashire and Cheshire, will number probably over 30,000. A meeting,to be addressed by the above gentlemen,will be held in the Great Hall of the Gardens, and an open- air meeting will be held on the Lake Shore, also to be addressed by them. A special train will leave Warrington Central Station at 12.58, fare ls. 3d. including admission to the gardens.

A poll of the members of the United States Senate shows that there is a majority in favour of a lock system canal across the Isthmus of Panama. The Premier stated on Wednesday !t was not likely that the Unemployed Bill could be introduced in time to pass through all its stages before the adjournment for the holidays. In addition to the Harrogate Convention it is probable that arrangements wilj, be made for another series of similar meetings at Cluiltenham, or Bristol for the Midlands and the 'West of England.

On Monday, Dan O'Connor, an elderly man, residing in Marsh-street, Widnes, was remanded for seven days on a charge of attempting to commit suicide by cutting his throat. On the 13th inst. a daughter of the lodging- house keeper heard a noise upstairs, and on going there she found the prisoner on his knees. She tried to raise him, but could not, and she went to bring her mother. On her return O'Connor had cut his throat with a razor. A WIDNES CHURCH CLUB.

• * * -*- With regard to the " Studio " murder, the " Tarer " says : " The police have shown great skill in investigating this crime. They have recon- structed every feature of this murder with the trifling exception of one small detail—the murderer." *s* Another week, and the great children's festival will once more be in full swing. The youngsters are already filled with gleeful anticipation of the day of days, and the Walking Day of 1906 promises to be quite as successful as any of the long series which have preceded it —given,' of course, fine weather. With such an enthusiastic band of workers, the arrangements for the great Cycle Parade cn July 21st are proceeding in admirable style. Warringtonians are promised a splendid spectacle and we may be sure that they will not overlook the highly deserving nature of the object—the extension of the Infirmary.

At Widnes on Saturday a Working Men's Club was opened in Hutchinson-street, one of tho poorest parts of the borough. The club, which has cost nearly £l,OOO, contains a large dining-room, gymnasium, baths, reading and writing room, tX.c. The vicar of St. Mary's (the Rev. G. Stephen Jones) and his Church Council are responsible for the experiment. The club is to be non- political and undenominational. A mission-room adjoins the club, and this was orrened on Saturday evening by the Bishop of Liverpool, who said that every church in the land should have a club connected with it where young and old could go.

* ** " Several local residents, who have latterly been I unable to secure employment, have been engaged to assist in the widening of Ditton Junctiop railway bridge, which is to commence immediately?'—This is the latest " society " intelligence from Cronton, published in a Widnes contemporary. * * * The Bridge-street improvements have made con- siderable progress of late, and some really handsome buildings have taken the place of those which have been demolished. When the widening is completed, the thoroughfare will be a credit to the town and more in keeping with the volume of traffic and the demands of a progressive community. _

A pleasing feature of Messrs. Crosfield's recreation scheme is the provision of garden allotments. These are being devoted to the cultivation of flowers and will add much to the attractiveness of the ground. It is interesting to note that most of the " gardeners" are girls who are particuarly enthusiastic in this matter.

* "It may he of interest," writes a Warrington correspondent to the "Liverpool Post and Mercury," "that we "heard the report of the explosion which occurred on the Haverford, and we are four miles east of Warrington, and about twenty-four miles from the Huskisson Dock. It was a still morning, and the sound made us think that one of the big guns at Seaforth had been fired."

* * * We are glad to note that the Education Committee is resolute in its intention to provide swimming instruction for the scholars attending the baths. The Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee, having refused to allow Mr. Barlow to act as instructor, the education authorities are seeking to introduce a paid instructor of their own. There should not, we imagine, be any objections to this course, and we congratulate the Education Committee on its determination to teach the children the very necessary art of swimming. * * _ _

Judging from •iie great headway which the Beauti- ful Warrington movement is making, Warrington will become a place of beauty much sooner than many of us had thought. The dullness of the streets has been pleasantly relieved by the display of window boxes filled with choice flowers, and neighbotirs are already exhibiting a friendly rivalry to obtain the brightest displays. We notice that the authorities of Bold-street Wesleyan Church have set an examole worthy of emulation, for the building has been very effectively embellished with window boxes and hanging baskets of flowers.

* * The reformation of Sankey-street is gradually nearing completion, and from all appearances the job will be a good one when finished. Tradesmen are of opinion, though, that it might have been completed sooner. Certainly, from personal observation we came to the conclusion that the men on the job would get through a lot of work in a lot of time. When one looked round one man was levelling the blocks with a delicacy of touch that would hardly have broken an egg. The others, some four or five, were conversing casually and apparently endeavouring to keep cool on a warm afternoon. *

The opening of . the splendid recreation ground which is henceforth to be the resort of Messrs. Cros- field's workpeople in the pleasant summer evenings marks quite a new departure as far as Warrington is concerned. Nicely situated and replete with every equipment for healthy sports, the ground could not be more suitable, and the employes and their friends may be relied upon to make the best possible use of it. There was only one disappointment about the opening ceremony, and that was the absence of Mr. A. H. Vrosfield, M.P., who telegraphed that indisposi- tion prevented his coming to Warrington on such a memorable occasion. *.* *_

Mr. Essex, the member for the Cirencester Division of Gloucester, has obtained the promise of a return to which other county members might suitably pay attention. This return is to give the number of Inclosures of Common land made under the Inclosures Acts from 1845 to 1509 in the county of Gloucester, with the acreage of these inclosures and other valuable particulars. There is no reason, Mr. Essex says, why similar returns should not be obtained for all counties, if only members ask for them in the usual way, and the information so furnished would obviously strengthen the hands of laud reformers all over the country. It would show that the land which we desire to restore to the people was first taken from the people. * * Young members of the House of Commons, especially if they are experienced and witty speakers, I should (says the "Daily Chronicle ") lay to heart the painful example of Mr. F. E. Smith, the Conservative member for Walton. He made what was by common consent the most brilliant maiden speech delivered in the House for years—indeed, as described in this column, since Lord Randolph Churchill. His wise course was thenceforward clear. Nothing on earth ought to have induced him to open his mouth again this session. Then he would have worn his unusual halo for a year. Instead of that, he • has spoken on every occasion, His second speech fell short ; his third fell flat ;on Monday—and before—he was a total failure. Now he has to climb up again to where he was when he first sat down. On Monday his only flash was an allusion to that " masterful and com- manding personality," the Under-Secretary to the Board of Education. Even Mr. Lough had to laugh at that. The rest was nothing. * * * " The Labour Party and the books that helped to make it "is the title of a number of illustrated inter- . views with Labour M.P.'s which is published in the ' current issue of the " Review of Reviews." It indicates very clearly the nature of the early struggles of those who are now engaged in making history in the House of Commons. Mr.,J. A. Seddon M.P. (Newton Division) described as a grocer's assistant and commercial travelled says : My boyhood was spent in a strong -Radical and Nonconformist home. The books chiefly the Bible, Carlyle, and Chartist literature. In early manhood I began to speak and study social questions, which brought me into contact with the Labour movement. I read anything and everything that came my way. Through a book club I secured a fair library, which contains Carlyle's works and most of the text books, or well-known authorities on social and Labour questions, and last but not least most of the poets. I think the first step to my present political views was prompted by Kidd's." Social Evolution." I cannot, however, give any special course adopted. I read a deal, did what I could for my class, and by accident got into Parliament,

div.head: ST, HELENS.
div.p: ST, HELENS.

LOCAL CHOIR'S SUCCESS. At the Lytham Musical Festival on Saturday. St, Helens Glee Club (conductor, Dr. S. Bertram Siddall) won the second prize in the competition for small male voice choirs. COMIC CYCLING AT ST. HELENS. • Martin Murray, of 82,College-street, was fined ss. and Costs at St. Helens, on Monday, on a charge of dis- orderly conduct. Police-constable O'Neill said he saw a crowd in College-street,and found it was attracted by Murray, who was drunk and riding a bicycle. He was rolling aboutthe road, and was nearly run over by a trap. The crowd followed into Corparation-street,jecr- ing at the man, and at the corner of Birchley-street he fell with the bicycle on the top of him. Thereupon he was locked up.

div.head: ST. HELENS SABBATARIANS.
div.p: ST. HELENS SABBATARIANS.

Mrs. Kate Seddon, of 7, Smithfield-street. Parr, was sent to gaol for twenty-eight days by the St. Helens magistrates, on Monday, for assaulting a neighbour, named Martha Johnson. The evidence was that Mrs. Seddon laid in wait for Mrs. Johnson at ten o'clock on Sunday night and assaulted her.—The Chief Constable said that Seddon must be a very violent woman, for she had twenty-five convictions and had been on indictment at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions for unlawful wounding. PRESENTATION TO THE VICAR. The Women and Girls' Bible classes connected with St. Helens Parish Church on Sunday presented to the Rev. Cyril Bardsley, vicar, a handsome replica, in silver of an old Roman rose bowl, on the pattern of a bowl found in the island of Gothland. The presentation was made at the Parochial Hall by Mrs. 111ssnett, in the presence of a gathering of about 600. Inside the bowl was inscribed "Presented by the Women and Girls' Bible classes to the Rev. C. C. B. Bardsley, M.A., and Miss Alice Gamble, 19th June, 1906." ST. HELENS MAN'S SHOCKING DEATH. Henry Brighouse, aged forty, of 3, Arnold-street, Peasley Cross, met with a painful death on Saturday at St. Helens. Brighouse was employed in connection with the Corporation Gasworks as a stoker, but on Saturday he was engaged painting the columns at the gasometer in Knowsley-road. He was seated in a swing seat, about half-past nine in the morning, about fifty feet from the ground, and could raise or lower himself by pulling the rope which was connected with a "snatch block." When he was hauling on the rope the whole thing came down, and he was thrown to the ground, having his hip dislocated and being seriously injured internally. He was conveyed to the St. Helens Hospital where his wife was already an in-patient. The poor fellow died on Saturday night, and leaves his sick wife with a family of nine or ten children, the oldest of whom is only fifteen years of age.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
HAYDOCK YOUTH'S SUCCESS.

Mr. W. F. Ireland, son of the vicar of Haydock, who has for five years been foundation scholar at Uppingham School, has been successful in winning the scholarship valued £5O per annum at St. John's College, Cambridge. A CHURCH INSTITUTE FOR EARLESTOWN.

Last Thursday evening at a meeting of the newly- formed branch of the Church of England ken's Society, held in the Mission Hall, a proposal was submitted and approved, for the establishment of a Church of England Men's Institute. Rev. A. Ainley, ALA., presided, and outlined the scheme. It was proposed to commence by renting a lock-up shop containing three or four rooms in Peel-street, to furnish and equip it as comfortably as possible for the purposes of reading, recreation, con- versation, &c. This will be the home of the C.E.M.S., and a centre for various kinds of parochial work. It was hoped to start early in the winter season, and to obtain a piano and semi-billiard table by then. By the generosity of Mr. Ainley the scheme was considerably helped forward, as he offered to make himself respon- sible for a year's rent in order to give the proposal a air start. Mr. W. Monks is the hon. secretary peo tent. COLLIERS v. CONSTABLES. James Dalton pleaded guilty to having been drunk at Burtonwood on June 9th, and was fined 2s. Gd. and costs. The following pleaded not guilty : John Kelly, Richard Kelly, Thomas Kelly, Thomas Dawson, Frederick Farimond, David Yates, and Michwl Giblin. Richard and Thomas Kelly were also charged with assaulting P.-c. Cartmell and damaging his uniform. Mr. Knowles defended them all. P.-c. Cartmell said there was a great disturbance in Chapel-lane that night, these and other men being drunk and some of them fighting. While he was trying to quell the distuabance two of the Kellys laid hold of him and threw him down, and in the struggle his trousers were torn. Mr. Knowles: What signs of drunkenness did you see? —They were all very drunk. Thomas Kelly went away 10 or 20 yards and then came back and butted me in the stomach. Richard Kelly threw me down and Thomas butted me.—Are you used to a colliery district ?—No. You have had BO experience of colliers before ?—Not inuch.—The Clerk: He has served his country and has got a medal. P.C. Cheethana, the other officer concerned gave similar evidence, and said they were struck several times. Richard Houghton, who helped the police to stop the disturbance, gave confirmatory evidence. The Chairman: Were they sober ? Mr. Knowles : Oh, they don't have to be sober, sir. The law allows them to be half-and-half. No doubt those who assaulted the police were drunk, or they would not have meddled with a policeman.—Mr. Knowles went on to say Dalton, Giblin, Yates, Farimond, and one of the Kellys, while , admitting that they had drink—as it was a Saturday— were not drunk. The policemen were new to the dis- trict and did not understand colliers' pastimes. There ; was no kicking of the police, and the men said there would have been no bother at all had not the police seized Thomas Kelly and attempted to handcuff him, ; instead of merely warning them, as older constables would have done. Then somebody shoved the police- men over, and Kelly got away and went home. He sub- , mitted that the men had done nothing of any consequence except that some of them were a bit drunk and one policeman's trousers got torn.—John Kelly was sworn and denied that he was drunk. He heard the crowd
bothering, but was going quietly past when one of thA 1„: •

bobbies nailed him and took hi s name. Farimond was also sworn, and said he had been to the "Limerick " and the " Bridge." He had nothing to do with the crowd outside the "Chapel House." Ile had had seven or eight half pint bottles of beer beeween and 11, and was not the worse for drink. Eight bottles in all the evening would not make him so.—James Dalton said he was first at the 'Limerick" and after- wards at the Chapel House.' He had about 4 bottles of beer, and afterwards 'a pint ; that was less than his usual Saturday allowance.—David Yates said he had about four pints. Double that amount would not have made him drunk.—Michael Giblin said he had 4 bottles of beer at the " Limerick " and a pint at the Chapel House." He was not drunk.—The defendants were fined 2s. Gd, each and costs, and Richard and Thomas Kelly ss. each for assaulting the constable, and the cost of mending his uniform. QUARREL BETWEEN APPRENTICES. At Newton Petty Sessions last Thursday Harold Bsrker, was summoned for assaulting Peter Ball on May 7th.—Mr. Arthur Browne, for the plaintiff,said the I parties were apprentices at the Viaduct Works, and the defendant had for some time been in the habit of throwing pieces of coke over the "bonnet" at the plaintiff. On May 7th, just before the buzzer blew for dinner,a piece of coke came over and only missed Ball's head because he ducked. He -went to the defendant and charged him with having thrown it. He denied it with bad language. As they were going home to dinner, the defendant bragged about what he would do to Ball if be hit him—which Ball had never threatened to do. Ball told him that if he did not abate his annoyace and his bad language he should do something. Some distance further on defendant stood over a stone in the roadway and told Ball that if he went near him he would split his --head. Ball, thinking he was going to throw it, went to him to take it away when the defendant first struck him with it and then threw it at him. div.p: Music In the Park. By the kind permission of Colonel Edelsten and officers commanding, the baud of the Ist Volu iteer Battalion (P.W.V.) South Lancashire Regiment will play an attractive programme of music in the Park on Sunday at 3.15 (weather permitting). 11.r.J.T.Richard- son will conduct. Auhletic Successes.

At the Manchester Police Sports on Saturday the five miles scratch race for the Cowley Cup was won by C, Berry, Warrington, who easily defeated T Sherratt, of Salford. Berry's time was 12oain. 26 1-ssecs. In the 220 yards at the Preston C.C. sports on Saturday P. Dunbobbia (114) was beaten by half a yard for the first place. -

Warrington Summer Camp. Rapid progress is being made in preparing the Warrington Summer Camp at Prestat3m for occupa- tion. As we recently announced the operations of the camp are ibeing considerably extended, and this year adults will be catered for at a low charge, in addition to the poor children. The camp opens on Walking Day. Warrington Bridge. The Town Council at its last meeting sanctioned the appointment of a sub-committee to inspect bridges constructed on the ferro-conerete principle with a view to considering its adoption in the case of Warrington Bridge. The committee have this week visited a bridge erected by Worcestershire County Council at Stanford and were favourably impressed with it. The committee intend to visit several other bridges and a full report will be presented to the Council.

Warrington P.S.A. There was a fair attendance at the weekly meeting of the Warrington Society which was held on Sunday Mr. Nicholson presided and delivered a short addres on" the importance of trifles." Mr. Joseph owen wa the speaker, and he delivered an address on "The true ideal of life." Miss Kendrick recited" The last hymn "in a very effective manner. Councillor Clegg read the Scripture lesson, and prayer was offered by Mr. R. Nelson. Mr. E Wynne Jones also took part in the service.

Srx-Gunma CYCLES. Excellent value. Call and inspect.—J. S. GARLAND,SI to 55, Bridge-st.—Acivt. , Death, of a Volunteer. ' Private W. Lee' D Company of the local Volunteer Battalion, having died at his residence in Warrington on the 19th inst., his remains will be interred with. ' military honours at the cemetery at two o'clock on Sunday afternoon. An escort consisting of one sergeant and 13 rank and file, under the command of Captain H. Owen, furnished if possible from D Company, will be in attendance. The regimental baud and other men:tilers of the battalion, including a firing party, will also take part in the procession.

div.head: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL. Annual Meeting If the Warrington and
div.p: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL. Annual Meeting If the Warrington and
District Association.

The annual meeting of the Warrington and District Football Association was held at the Patten Arms hotel on Thursday evening under the presidency of Quarter-master Sergeant J. P. Hollins. There was a good attendance of representatives of the various clubs. THE REPORT. Mr. T. P. BRADSHAW, the retiring hon. secretary presented the report as follows :—The Association last season was divided into five divisions and the number of clubs in each division was as follows :—Warrington 11, Cheshire 12, Earlestown 3, St. Helens 2 and Widnes 2, making a total membership of 30 Clubs against 25 the previous season an increase in membership of 5 clubs. Out of that number IG entered for the "Observer" Challenge Cup as against 12 the previous season. This competition again proved to be a great source of attraction to the followers of the Associa- tion game, the matches being well patronized particularly in the semi-final and final ties. After many attempts the cup was won by Oughtrington Park arter a hard fight with Northwich Victoria. The services of Mr. Kingscott, a member of the Football Association, were secured as referee for the final tie, and his engagement proved a distinct success. Eighteen meetings of the Executive have been held during the past season, and the Emergency Committee have met on three occasions, The attendance of the members of the Executive has been excellent, and they deserve special praise for the manner in which they have dis- charged their duties during the past season. Twenty- one cases of misconduct have been ronorted during the past season, and dealt with as follows :-1 case was dismissed ; S players cautioned ; 4 suspended for 7 days ; 4 for 14 days; 1 for 21 days ; 1 for a month, and 1 for 2 months, and 1 player is under suspension pending appearance, three clubs were cautioned for disorderly conduct, one club Was ordered to having warningnotices issued by the Football Association posted on the Ground. One club was fined for playing a player daring suspension. Two Club Secretaries have also been suspended for misconduct. Two benefit matches were sanctioned. Fins cially we are in a sound position and building up a good reserve fund. The total income during the past season has been £43 17s. lid., which with balance in hand from season 1901-5 brings the receipts to £5O 4s. id. The nett gain on the Cup Competition was ,C:11 Ss. ad. The expenses during the past season amount to £26 2s. Gd. leaving a balance in ' hand of £54 is. 7d. Mr. J. Fulton Smith is again nominated for the position as President, and the interest he has taken in the work of the Association during the past two seasons is well known to all of you. The Chairman, Quartermaster-Sergeant J. P. Hollins is also nominated fore-election and I can safely say that much of the success of the Association is due to the tact and sound judgment displayed by him on all occa- sions. Mr. G. T. Bibby, a member of the Executive for the past two seasons, is nominated for Treasurer and Mr. R. P. Booth as Secretary. I do not offer m3ielf for re-election owing to circumstances well known to you all but in giving tip my official position as Secre- tary, I beg to thank the members of the Executive,Club Secretaries, referees and players for the kindness extended to me during my ten years' connection with the Associktion and in return I can only say my services j are at your disposal whenever required. The CHAIRMAN in moving the adoption of the report expressed regret at the retirement of Mr. Bradshaw and said that only those who had been officially connected with the work of the Association could fully realize the loss of his services. In Mr. Booth, however, he would have a worthy successor. He (the chairman)was afraid Mr. Booth would not always find it work of the most pleasant nature, but they could hardly expect that •! Mr. SMALLEY seconded and the report was adopted. ELECTIONS. On the motion of Mr. HARVEY seconded by Mr. J. A. B tsKe, the following officers were elected :—President, Councillor J. Fulton Smith ; chairman, Quartermaster- sergeant, J. P. Hollins ; hon. treasurer, Mr. C.T. Bibby; hon. secretary, Mr. R.B.Booth. With regard to the election of the executive, the following nominations were -eceived from the War- rington division :—Mr. W. H. Smalley (Post Office Athletic) ; Mr. J. A. Banks (Latchford Christ Church) • Mr. George Bowman (Warrington Albions) ; Mr. C. r. Cox (St. Barnabas'). The last-named club not having paid their subscription the nomination of Mr. Cox watt inadmissible and the other gentlemen were elected. For the Cheshire division Mr. A. J. Titmns (Daresbary) was elected. Earlestown, Widnes, and St. Helens did not submit nominations. PROPOSED ALTERATION OF RULES. Mr. WOODS, on behalf of the Warrington Albions, moNied an alteration of rule 17 to provide that the maximum amount to be paid by the Association for the use of club grounds should be 20 per cent. en the gross gate, instead of 10 per cent, as at present. He con- tended that as the balance in hand was substantial the clubs ought to derive sortie benefit. Mr. BRADSHA w objected to the alteration on behalf of the Association. He said the maximum which the English Fogtball Association allowed for the use of grounds was 10 per cent. • There was no seconder to the motion, which therefore fell to the ground. Mr. WOODS then moved with regard to the Cup com- petition :—" In each semi-final and final tie, the Asso- ciation shall after paying all expenses take one-third of the net proceeds, the remainder to be equally divided between thecompeting teams." Mr. BRADSHAW said a similar rule was once in opera- tion, but it did not work satisfactorily. It would, he thought, be far better to offer gold medals for com- petition instead of giving the clubs an increased share of the rate. The CHAIR:kr AN said he had always strongly advocated the offering of gold medals, and he could promise that the subject would receive serious attention this season, On that misunderstanding Mr. WOODS withdrew his motion.

THE CHAIRMAN AND cranes. A..vote of thanks was accorded to the retiring Execu- tive Committee, the CHAIRMAN expressing regret that Mr. Foulkes had severed his connection with executive work. Continuing, he said he was sorry that some of the gentlemen who had written to the papers criticising the working of the Association had not been nominated for they would then have found that the Association was ruled in a fair spirit. Apparently the critics were not connected with any club or they would have been anxious to take part in the management of the Association. Mr. BRADSHAW : It does not effect any of us. I Mr. HARVEY moved a vote of thanks to the chairman and officials and paid a tribute te the work of Mr. Bradshaw, who, he said, was retiring with honour to himself and to the Association. The vote was heartily accorded and in responding the CHAIRMAN said he hoped.... it would be possible to arrange for some first class League club to play a match with a picked team from the Association, the proceeds to be devoted to the Infirmary extension fnnd,

Marriage of the Rev. F. C. Bozman. An interesting ceremony took place at Lyman schools on Saturday evening, when a presentation was made to the Rev. F. C. Bozman, curate of Lyman Church, who has been appointed Vicar of New Springs, Haigh. The present consisted of a silver salver, suitably inscribed, a cheque for £lOO, and an illuminated address, containing the, names of the subscribers. There was a large attendance over which Mr. A. Welkin presided. Mr. Callender, who made the pre- sentation spoke of the good feeling which existed amongst the parishioners towards Mr. Bozman and expressed the hope that his married life would be a happy one.—Mr. John Coxon said the subscription list was a representative one, and there were 210 subscribers, which testified to the good feeling existing between the parishioners, Mr. Bozman and the Rector.—Mra. C. E. Cowper, T. Ardern, J. T. Milnes and H. S. Saville also spoke.—Mr. Bozman suitably replied.— The committee who bad in hand the testimonial were Dr. Barrows (hon. secretary), and Messrs. John Coxon (hon. treasurer), A. W. Callender, W. P. Mackendrick, H. S. Saville. and Fred E. Evans. —A presentation 'was made to Mr. Bozman on Sunday in tbe vestry by the choir. It took the form of a study chair and was I made by Mr. Mathers (organist) addresses being also given by Messrs. J. W. Wyatt and H. Pearson. The bellringers presented Mr. Bozman with a dinner gong, and the teachers and scholars of the school with a couple of pictures. Mr. Bozman's wedding took place quietly soon after eight o'clock on Monday at the Parish Church. The bride is Miss Margaret Bayley, younger daughter of Mr. William Bayley, Craybrow, Lyman.
