the crowded street and could not help herself. Some- how, she said, she got into a doorway, and there she sat until the crowd had gone by. She lay out of doors two nights and lost all she had. One fellow was caught cutting the, ears of a woman for her earrings. Two soldiers got hold of him and swung him into the fire. That was the last of him. Cutting fingers off for rings, and all such horrid work as only such devils as 'Frisco has in it could do. My own experience was horrid enough, but I saw none of this. My situation was in the great railroad yard. In one of its ware- houses I was the fire signalman. The warehouses make up one side of the yard, the other side was a long street of big furniture, agriculture, wool and meat . warehouses. These latter were all on fire pretty well at once. A little further on was an immense pile of office building belonging. to the railroad, and then the big patent medicine works all seemed to be ablaze at once. At one time I was up between these blazing buildings and. the cars, and I had to run. I thought my clothes would surely catch on, my whiskers and my face were anything but cool, when I got Clear. Oh, I shall never forget that night. When the fire got near the Great Western Meat Company Warehouses, the dews were thrown open, and the people told to help themselves, and the sight of the crowds rushing in and carrying away the meat added something auggestive of the Christian's hell and all its devils. One man hurrying by me had four hams he was struggling with. " Hear Harry," he shouted, " take one,l cannot carry the lot." I took one, and a good joh'l did—it was the only bit of meat we had for many a day. Yes, that was a fire to remember. Some of these warehouses were stored with oil, and when these caught on, and the black dense smoke joined with the smoke from the wool and again. with.the furniture, the sight was one only lan artistic Dante could picture, of certainly some- one with a better Inferno acquaintance than I have. You see the fire seems to have crowded the earthquake out. The money loss was so great, but the central horror remains with the quake all the same. And then there was the night on the hills, all around were people whose homes were burning. Worse, there were hundreds who were separated from kith and kin,not knowing what the fire was consuming in its mad fury. No water, no anything—driven into the hills with just the clothes on their backs, and up those hills I struggled with my poor old legs and the ham on my shoulder, I think this is about the last talk I shall commit unless there is some new develop- ment, but I am hoping for the best and I have the best wife in all creation to help me along. She is as brave as any that are made now-a.days. I am pleased to say my legs are somewhat better, and as I have got a job that has no work tied to it and is worth 60 dollars a month, I think I shall stay -with it, that is if that qld beldame Dame naturo is willing. Where we live is really beautiful. Flowers are all around the house, what's underneath lam not quite sure about I think we are likely to stay in lodgings some time yet. There are no houses to let and rents are going up out of sight—Your loving brother,
H. WHITIIAM, 2,855, Jackson-street, Alameda, California.

div.head: FASHIONABLE WEDDING AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: FASHIONABLE WEDDING AT ST. HELENS.
Miss A. Gamble Marries the Vicar.

The people of St. Helens held high festival on Tues- day. when a general holiday prevailed throughout the town in honour of the marriage of the Rev. Cyril Charles Bowman Bardsley (vicar of St. Helens), third son of the Rev. Canon Bardsley, Sidcup, Kent formerly vicar of Huddersfield), to Miss Alice Gamble, fourth daughter of Sir David Gamble, Bart, K.C.B. The bride has always taken the deepest interest in church work, and has, among other things, done a great deal of work among the girls at Parr, as well as in connection with the Parish Church. The enthusiasm in the streets was remarkable, and could hardly have been greater at a Royal visit. It was really a good and striking display of popular affection. The line of route from Windle- hurst to the church was decorated with gaily-waving flags, and Church Street was gorgeous with lines of flags crossing and re-crossing from the church to the opposite buildings. The interior of theHrtilding was bright and attractive with the brilliant sunshine streaming through the handsome stained-glass windows, and in the chancel were groups of madonna and harrisii lilies among ferns and palms, whilst the choir stalls were bordered with pale green foliage and clusters of dracenas and asaleas. The service was fully choral, the church choir being augmented by that from St. Mary's Mission Church, under the conductorship of Mr. Wood- ward, organist. The officiating clergy were the .Bishop of Liverpool (Dr. Chavasse), the Rev. Canon Bardsley (father of the bridegrogm), the Rev. Canan Willink (vicar of Great Yarmouth, formerly vicar of St. Helens), and the Rev. Arthur Gamble (vicar of Bradbonrne, (Derbyshire.) brother of the bride. The best man was Mr. G. T. Tomlinson, barrister, of London, and the stewards in church-were Mr. David Gamble, jun., Mr. Hugh Gamble. Mr. Norman Gamble, the Rev. Ernest Bardsley, and the Rev. John Eyre. The bride, who was given away by her father, wore a handsome gown of ivory moire silk trimmed with ruchings of chiffon and draped with exonisite Italian lace, the gift of her sister, Miss Gamble. The bodice was covered with the lace, and the amethyst and pearl necklace, a present from Mrs. Edward Jackson. London, formed a charming ornament on the soft folds of lace. The bridal veil was secured by a diamond and pearl brooch, the gift of the bride's sister, Mrs. Hammilhand the present from the bridegroom was a diamond ring. The bride cluried a magnificent shower bouquet of white roses and lilies. The bridesmaids were Miss Josephine Henrietta Gamble (niece), Miss Anna Dorothea Carr (niece), Miss Enid Kathleen Gamble (niece)—all goddaughters of the bride—Miss Pamela Redmayne, and Miss Kathleen Bardsley (niece of the bridegroom). They 'wore dainty frocks of white muslin and Valenciennes lace. made Empire style, and white lace mushroom hats, with knots of pink ribbon. They carried lovely baskets of pink • roses, and wore enamelled monogram brooches, the gifts of the bridegroom. The service began with the hymn " Thine for ever," and after the ceremony the wedded pair were addressed by the Bishop. Outside the church traffic was suspended for the bridal procession' and the throngs of eager sightseers were kept in admirable order by the police, some of whom were mounted for the first time in St. Helens. The admirable arrangements for the perfect control of the crowds that lined the thoroughfares were perfectly carried out under Chief Constable Ellerington. The long drive to the house was lined by some 2.000 children from the day and Sunday parochial schooll,the girls in white frocks and posies of flowers, boys and girls wearing a commemoration medal, and gave lusty cheers as bride and bridegroom passed in an open carriage. The children remained whilst all the guests drove past, and their clear ringing voices sounded pleasantly across the park. On the lawns the Euterpean Ladies' Orchestra performed an excellent programme as the company strolled along the lovely grounds after congratulating the newly-wedded couple. The numerous guests were received by Miss Gamble, whose fawn voile gown was worn with a hat trimmed with pale green shaded feathers, and she carried a bouquet of damask roses. The Rev. C. C. B. Bardsley and Mrs. Bardsley left ' during the aften.oon for London, en route for Switzer- land, where the honeymoon is to be passed. The bride trivelled in a costume of pale grey cloth, and a three. cornered hat trimmed with clusters of shaded blossoms.

div.head: ANOTHER LETTER FROM MR. H. WHITHAM.
div.p: ANOTHER LETTER FROM MR. H. WHITHAM.
WORKSHOP TRAGEDIES.
The Story of a Tailoress who was rescued from despair by Bile Beans.

IThe conditions under which thousands of wonobn workers have to live and labour day after day and year after yearS are not conducive to perfect happiness. The I close stuffy air of the workroom or the mill, the buzz and clatter of mschinery, the high temperature,the long ; hours and the hasty meals, are enough to break down I the strongest of constitutions. The incessant strain finds out the weak spot, the constitutional failing, and j then comes the breakdown and the tragedy. To a local ; reporter Mrs. Jennie Thompson, of 6, Bank-street, Boar- lane, Leeds, recently told how Bile Beans averted such a tragedy in her life. I "I am a tailoress, and my work requires the use of I gas-heated irons," said Mrs. Thompson. "I suffered with such extreme weakness and giddiness that the I room appeared to be going round and round. My face was entirely covered with nasty spots, which quite dis- figured me.. I had no appetite whatever, a heavy weight on my chest, and a nasty taste in my mouth. "For seven. years I bad these breakdowns and they I became so serious that I had treatment for dye months from an eminent doctor, but I became worse. I tried 1 pills for my head and patent soaps for my face, but still I did not improve. My weight was greatly reduced A friend recommended Bile Beans, and after taking 1 them for some time the dizziness ,and pains on the chest guite disappeared, and the spots on my face were I all gone. I can now enjoy my food, and have put on I flesh very rapidly. I am now quite strong and well I again, thanks to Bile Beans. For biliousness, indigestion, constipation' and all ailments arising from liver, stomach, or bowel disorders Bile Beans are an absolute cure. div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Queen Victoria of Spain.—The Queen of Spain is to be known in history as Queen Victoria, which is the most appropriate as well as being the first of her baptismal names. Such was not the name with our late Queen, whose first name was Alexansbuna, but this was dropped because it was thou:lit that a Russian name would not commend itself to popular favour in this country. For a similar reason the Queen of Spain could not adopt her second name Enenie, which would be unpopular in Spain, because of its French origin. The Queen of Spain could have no better name than that which our late revered Queen made a syno-iym with all that was good, and it pleases the Spanish people. There are i many people n this country who think that the young Queen is scarcely living up to the best traditions of her honoured namesake by presiding over bull fights and attending pigeon shooting matches, but she at least is not responsible for the national sports of her adopted country, and it is difficult to see what else she can do, but to acquiesce in them. Royal Ascot. —Ascot parties were scarcely so numer- ous as usual, although the King had a number of guests at Windsor Castle for the meeting of the fashionable world of sport on the Berkshire Downs. The absence of the Queen and also of the Prince and Princess of Wales to attend the Coronation of the King, and Queen of Norway, bad some effect in keeping people away and the meeting was shorn of its customary semi-state pageantry. Prince and Princess Christian had a small party including Lord and Lady Cadogan at Cumberland Lodge and the Duke and Duchess of Devonshire have been at Fern Hill, the guests of Mr. and Mrs. Arthur Sassoon. The Duchess of Newcastle had a party at Bishop's Farm, near Windsor, and so did Mrs. Adair at Englefield Green. Prominent among the fashionable element of the meeting was the large number of Americans, nearly everyone of the principal houses in the neighbourhood contributing its quota 'of visitors, representative of American Society, and everywhere there was evidence of the ousting of smart equipages by the modern motor car. The latter has now firmly established itself as a fashionable necessity in tgisto- cratic families and although there are a few whcf still remain entirely faithful to their horses, the number is a constantly diminishing one, and many who were at first most opposed to the motor car are now amongst its most enthusiastic patrons. _ _ _

The Suffragist Agitatora—The Marauess of North- ampton who vainly tried to pacify the women suffragists at Mr. Asquith's meeting at Northampton is a practical , writer, as well as a fine platform speaker. He is one I of the small band of Liberal peers, but in spite of this I and his great local influence, his presence on the plat- I form did not protect the Chancellor of the Exchequer from the interruptions of the saffragistagitators. They I look upon Mr. Asquith as the chief opponent in the I Cabinet to their cause—and it looks as if he will require the constant protection of the police until these women agitators recognise that they are doing infinite harm to their cause by resorting to methods of violence and disorderly conduct. An Old-time Romance.—The Compton family, of which the Marquis of Northampton is the head, derive I the greater part of their immense wealth from estates i in a densely populated district in the north of London, ! and for these they are indebted to the kindly interven- tion of Queen Elizabeth. The property originally I belonged to Sir John Spencer. Once Lord Mayor of London, whose daughters, William Compton, afterwards the first Earl wanted to marry. Sir John, for .some reason, was opposed to his suit and took great pre- cautions to prevent a runaway match' which, in the days , of romance, was generally expected in such ()helm- I stances. According to the story however, William I Compton gained admittance to the house disguised as a I workman, and eventually bore off his lady love in a ' basket. The wealthy merchant would have nothing more to do with them,but after a time Queen Elizabeth sent for him, and suggested that he should adopt a cer- tain little girl, in place of his disinherited daughter. , She, of course was Sir John's own little granddanghter, 1 a reconciliation folloitred, and in the end the rich old I merchant left his son-in-law all his property. 1 Pit Door-Enthusiasts.—The eccentric amusements in; which some people delight, have been a favourite subject 1 with the satirists of all ages, and itifs probable that if ' Horace had lived in our time he would have had some- thing to say concerning such incidents as were observed last week outside Drury-lane Theatre. If ever there as an occasion whieh called for some special effort on the part of theatre goers, it was surely that of the Ellen Terry jubilee celebration, but nevertheless it is a little difficult to understand such enthusiasm as that which prompted many women and a few men to wait outside the pit door for more than 24 hours, in order to I obtain admission. The record of this strange competi- tion was secured by A lady who tobk up her position. at 6.30 a.m. fora performance on the following afternoon. i It may be supposed that one such experience s sufficient to last a person a lifetime, but that was not the first occasion. upon which such grotesque heroism had been witnessed, and it is scarcely likely that it will be the last. Possibly if these enthusiasts were consulted, they might suggest that they were not the only people who take their pleasures strangely. They rnightreven point to the Lancushire men who trevellsd 40 hours in order to spend 14 in Paris, and to the party from London who this week took a day trip to Ostend and back. 0-The Instalment System.—A few London modisteeare now offering to dress their customers on the instalment System, but is to be ionbted whether the notion will "catch on." A certain sum is fixed upon which covers the entire year, and this is paid quarterly. The customer binds herself to buy everything from the modiste, and the modiste on her part agrees to provide whatever is required by the customer up to the value of the quarterly cheque. The idea was evolved in the hope of doing away with the long credit system. and abolishing the trouble of obtaining ,even stop-gap monies from "smart " dressers,but there are many difficulties in the way of making the plan a success, which already modistes and customers seem to have discovered. Feather Boas.—When we were told at the commence- ment of the season that an epidemic of feather boas would fall to our lot this summer,few probably.realized the exterit to which we should become victims. The woman or girl minds a feather boa, whether ostrich, marabout, or a skilful admixture of the latter, and chiffon or lace, is „a curiosity, and a certain " smart," r dresser has now succeeded in creating a sensation, by first encircling the brown of her hat with the finest and most magnificent ostrich feather boa, next allowing it to fall behind, and then,drape itself about the shoulders toward the front, from whence it falls almost to the feet. The ieea is not likely to recommend itself even to those who can afford it, the effect being heavy and decidedly "overdone." Moreover the mode is certainly calculated to impede all graceful movements of the head. Millinery Grapes.—Dull black grapes set in little black leaves are finding favour with the milliners and bad they hunted round for years they could scarcely have hit upon a more hideous notion. With the lovely purple varieties we are all familiar, and these are again to the fore,mingled/with the pale green or white species but they are not so modish as the heavy inartistic mingling of black grapes and leaves. '
MADGE.

div.p: WOMAN'S REALM.
DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
LADY CARE'S NEW EMBROIDERIES.

Lady Carew and her sister, Mrs. Cory, whose artistic talent is of a high order, may be found on most forenoons, even in the height of the season, at their embroidery frames in the chercij morning-room of Lord Carew's house in Bel- grave-square. Lady Carew is embroigering in coloured silks on a light ground a 3et of covers for the drawing-room furniture, while her sister is engaged on a large panel. Mrs. Cory's won- derful reproduction in embroidery of Burne- Jones's elaborate painting. "Muss a," is now a notable object in the front drawilic-room, no less than faces and seven full length figures being. realistically depicted. Mrs. Cory, who in technique and expression could "give points and a beating" to many profe.sional pianistes, has lately taken up some quaint spinet music, which she plays with all her accustomed charm. QUAINT LITTLE FROCK FOR CHILD.

The original of the quaint little linen frock worn by the child in our sketch was fashioned in a pretty shade of shrimp-pink, and was worn over a guirnpe of pink-and-white check muslin. The tunic was laid in box-pleats back and front, the square neck being finished with a series of

buttoned 'scallops, and it was caught into the waist by a sash of wide pink satin ribbon, tied in a bow in front. The tunic fell over an underskirt of the same pink linen, and the pretty little epau- lette sleeves, with their scalloped edges, were quite short enough to shew. the guimpe sleeves of the check muslin reaching just to the elbow.

div.head: WEARING OF "COLONES."
div.p: THE WEARING OF "COLONES."

The assertion that women have almost aban- doned the pretty custom, handed to us froth a more chivalrous age, of wearing the "colours" of favoured members of the opposite sex is true to a certain extent, writes "Miranda," but that club colours, racing colours, and regimental colours have still an attraction in feminine eyes is proved upon many occasions each season. One need only cite such instances as regimental races, the "eights weeks" at the universities, the public school and university cricket matches at Lord's, and Henley Regatta, to recall that colours are bravely " sported" which at any other time would be banished. Very often the allegiance of fair partisans has proved the de- spair of dressmakers, who are called upon to make the best of chromatic combinations at which their patrons would shudder protestingly if asked to contemplate as a question of taste. It is too late, however, to regret that feminine counsel was not taken before the jaundiced mix- tures of hues which constitute the badge of many of the leading clubs were decided upon.

SMART FLANNEL COSTVILE. It is always a good thing for the majority of the fair sex when Dame Fashion elects to put stripes to the fore, since stripes tend to lengthen a figure and make it appear slimmer and younger than is actually the case; so we cannot wonder that this summer the stripe is introduced into every variety of material. In flannels we/ find some very dainty shades patterned with a thread stripe in a darker tint, and these are made up into the most effective little costumes

for river, tennis, and general holiday Sr. Our sketch chews a model recently seen and repro- duced for this column. It was of palest green flannel, with a dark stripe, And the useful round skirt was simply trimmed with three bands of the material cut on the cross and piped round the edges. The little slack coat hung from a yoke, which was piped and tabbed along the lower edge, the coat itself being laid in groups of small tucks, and held-down at the waist by a leather belt, the full sleeves being finished with a strapped band at the wrist.

div.head: PAIRED FOR DIVISION.
div.p: PAIRED FOR DIVISION.

Mr. Walter Long, the other day in the House of Commons, says P.T.0., Mr. T. P. 0-Connor's new paper, drew a pathetic picture of a house- hold divided 'against themselves as a result of Woman's Suffrage vhers it came to wives voting against their husbands. At the I.L.P. Con- ference it was noticed that on the voting for the • place of meeting next year, Mrs. Snowden voted for Buxton, while Mr. Snowden, M.P., voted for Edinburgh. "Great Scott" muttered Mr. Snowden, ,"see how my wife is voting," and then lie signalled to her, A slight flush suffused her face as she smiled back again, but her hand was still up in support of Buxton. "Women," said -Mr. Snowden, regretfully, '! ought never to haye votes." Is it, asks P.T.0.. that Mr. Long is Ilso of the sons of the prophets?

div.head: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.
div.p: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.

CrCUMBER MAYONNAIM—Take three or four early cucumbers, peel them and cut them in two, lengthways, removing / the seed with a spoon. Cut some very thin slices of cold roast beef— lean and a little underdone—and spread them on both sides with .French mustard. ',Boil two eggs hard, remove the yolks, passing them through a sieve, and chop up the 17/bites finely. Take some bottled anchovies, soak them in milk for half an hour, and then rub into a smooth paste with tho yolk of erg and a spoonful of mixed parsley. Put the slices of beef on the lower halves of the cucumbers, seas& with salt and pepper, and spread with a layer of the anchovy mixture. Plane another lever of beef on the tom „mink!e witn inincea gnemins, cover wun rue orner, halves of the cucumbers, and pour a thick mayonnaise sauce over all, covering the top with grated tongue.

MY pEart CrizrzßEN, Many of you have written me letters tell- ing me how you spent your few days' hcliday at Whitsun, and I hope next week to publish a few of these letters, if I can find space in these columns. I am pleased to hear that all your gardens seem to be such a great success, and I gather that some of you are also growing lettuces, radishes, etc. This I think an excel. lent idea; perhaps, next year I shall arrange for a vegetable competition instead of flowers. I have ineerted a few puzzles below, sent Toe by one of my nieces. I will give a prize to the one sending me the first correct solutions. You will see that they are quite easy, and I think all of you could try to guess them The time is getting near for you to send me your monthly competition's, and I hope all those who have not already sent me some- thing will do so at once; if you could see the nice prizes that await the winners, I am sure every one would send me a cdntribution. I am sending a prize this week to Thomas Thacker for his contribution; this was very neatly and nicely written. With all good. wishes from.your affectionate UNCLE NED.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l am sending you a short contribution for the "Children's Corner League," entitled THE BIRDS ROME ONCE MORE. It is the beauteous month of May, ' The cuckoo's voice is loud and clear; The brooklet wand'ring on its way Is singing to the willows near. At early morn the blackbird's notes Ring from the tree-tops waving high, The skylark's matin downward bloats In joyous music from the sky. Swallows and martins once again Have sought our isle from Afric's shore, _ _
And swiftly skim o'er hill and plain To seek the home they left before.

What joy is theirs! A happy pair , Of martins find their last year's nest, Or part of it, and soon repair The home belov'd, wherein to rest. 'Tis but a shabby little spot, \ A homesteadhuilt of mud and clay; \ But they, contented with their lot, Are lining it with straw or hay. And so these masons of the air, Swift circling o'er the sheltering eaves, _ .

Will soon rebuwild with loving care s Their nest above the ivy leaves. And, twittering to eaclh other low, After their flight from distant shore, Will say, "How sweet it is to know That we are home again once more." From your affectionate nephew, T. THAcxzg.
PUZZLES FOR PLAYTIME. BURIED BOYS' AND GIRLS' NAMES. 1. On the box was marked Win large letters. 2. Tell her, if she lends me the book, I will not
- - keep it long. 3. Remember that you come early to-morrow. 4. Addrese the letter, Mr. Reed, gardener and florist. 5. I found last night in the cab a silver bracelet.

'Uncle Ned,—You will think I have for- ptten you a:id that I do not take any interest in the "Children's Corner," but I have been away from home for about nine weeks, and so I could not very well 'write to you. I do not think I have told you Ufa I ar deaf. I got deaf through 'scarlet fever for years ago. I have had several things done me, but it ddd not do any good, eo I,have bf
leen

to see a specialist in London, to see if he could do anything for me, but he could not, and so I shall have t 6 go to a school to learn lip-reading. I am going to one at the end of August. My mother has saved the "Children's Cor- ner' for me, and so I can tell what competi- tions you are having. I hope it is not too late for this letter about my holidays at, Easter, be- cause I went away on March 12th, and came back May 9th. Now I will tell you about my holidays. I went to London with some relatives, who were staying at Poole, so I left when they went to London. I did not go straight to London., but I stayed at Southampton for four days. I saw many interesting places while I was there. One day I had a drive all round the town. I passed under the Bargate, and then I went in the docks. There were several very large ships —the largest I have ever seen. The one I liked best was a whit e one; its name is "Aasaye." It sailed for South\Africa two days after. When I came out of the 'docks, I passed the pier, Old Walls, and went on the Western Shore. passed the "Stella" Fountain, and I went to several other old places. Have you ever been , there, Uncle Ned? After my stay of four days, I went to Southfields. I stayed there for three weeks. I often went to Putney, and one day I went on Putney Bridge to see Oxford and Cambridge crew practice for the race. 'Wimble- don Common is not far from where I stayed, and my/cousin and friends often went there and had'aice games, and sometimes hadVicnice there. It has two lakes, "Kingsmere " and "Que,ensmere," about h.alf-a-mile apart from each other. .It has also a large windmill, and an old Roman well, Julius Cresar. The Common is about six miles, I believe, and I have been all over it. After my three weeke' stay' at South- fields,4 I went to Upper Holloway. I went by motor !bus, and so I could see a nice lot of places. I passed a lot of monuments, Picca- dilly Curcus, and Earl's Court. I saw the Big Wheel at Earl's Court, etc. I went tb see, the specialist at Upper Holloway. I was there for Easter. I went to a lot of places. It was very nice at Waterloo Park, at Highgate, and Par- liament Hills (you can see a good view from the summit),and at Waterloo Park there is a dial which is at exact level with St. Paul's dome, so I must have been very high up. I stayed there for three weeks, and then went back to Southfielde. While I was at South- fields, I went to St. Paul's Cathedral. • • My cousin and I went with a. lady. We went by train to Waterloo. We went over Waterloo Bridge. I saw Westminster Abbey and the Houses of Parliament, and the Hotels Cecil, and Savoy, near the Thames. We walked to St. Paul's along the river, but we came back a different way, down Ludgate Hill. We passed one or two colleges, the Law Courts, and a lot more places. It was St. Paul's Sunday School anniversary, and there were about 7,520 children present (I believe that is the exact number). I came back to Poole, on May sal, through lovely country. It was a long way back. It took 44 hours (I came back with some relatives). We went to Waterloo first, and took train from there, and we did not change until we got to Salisbury, and from there to t'uole. I was told that the train travelled at 70 miles an hour. I am much better for my long holiday. It is the longest I have ever had away from Poole. I have visited three places in nine weeks—Southampton, Southfield/a, and Hollo- way._

I hope you will like this letter, and it is not too long to print; if it is too long to print this wsek, please continue the week after if you can. I should like to join in the Flower ,Show Competition, but I was back too late to plant the seedo in time. I have a garden, and many flowers in it—pansies, wallflowers, London Pride, bluebells, and a lot more, which I can- not stop to tell you now, so I must clo.se now, with beet wislates. Yours truly,
GLADYS.

ENIGMA. My first is in croquet, but not in garlic My second is in picture, butsnot in frame. My third is in silver, but not in gold. My fourth is in heat, but not in cold. My fifth is in honey, but not in bee. My sixth is in wave, but not in sea. My sevengt is in daisy, but' not in flower. My eighth is in castle, but not in tower. My ninth is in sunlight. but not in shade. My tenth is in trowel, but not in spade. 3,1 y eleventh is in miser, but not in wealth. My twelfth is in sickness, but not in health. My thirteenth is in gauntlet, but not in glove. My whole is a lady we dearly love. From MARGARET SABLE.
Dear Uncle Ned,—l look at my seeds every day, and they are coming up nicely. I am sending you a piece of poetry, which I hope 'will be suitable to print. It is called "THE COTTAGER TO HER INFANT."

The days are cold, the nights are long; The north wind sings_ a doleful song. Then hush again upon my breast.— All merry things are, now at rest, Save thee, my pretty love! The kitten sleeps upon the hearth; The crickets long have ceased their tairth— There's nothing stirring in the house Sa.i7e one wee, hangry, nibbling mouse. .4. Then why so busy thou? say! start not at that sparkling light: 'Tie but the moon that shines so bright On the window-pane, bedropped with rain; Then, little darling, 'sleep again, And wake when it is day.

Dear Uncle Ned,—lt gives me great pleasure in writing you anuther letter. I hope you are quite well, and enjoyed your Whitsun holidays. I am pleased to see what a lot of nieces and nephews you have, and how they all try to help and make interesting "The Children's Corner."
I saw in last week's, that you wanted a piece lf poetry, so I am sending jou one, although am afraid it is rather short.
_ • I:, is of my own composing, and I hope you will think it good enough to put in the Corner."
Now I ,muct close my letter. Hoping to see my poem in print,
I remain your loving Niece, PAITA MEWETT.
BRITANNIA..

Britannia, the pride of the ocean; Britannia, the pride of our lands. How well does she look. on her gilded throne. With the sceptre of office in hands. Tho' she is small as a country, Tho' she is but a speck, • She can fight the foes who oppress her, On battlefield or on dec. • She keeps in her hand the roll-call of fame—.
Of heroes now dead and gone. But, tho' they are dead, we must not forget That they died for Britannia's name.
FAITTI MEWETT.

div.head: An Up-to-Date Cycle Factory.
div.p: An Up-to-Date Cycle Factory.

The modern manufacturing methods employed by the New Hudson Cycle Co., of Birmingham, have been interestingly described by a recent visitor to their works, which latter are now twelve times the size they were ten years ago. Employing 1,100 hands, with a wages bill of £60,000 per annum, the 'New Hudson output is 1,600 complete machines a week, and the total for this year it is estimated ,will reach 40,000. By means of ingenious auto- matic machines, rough forgings in the semblance of cranks are converted into the finished article, four at a time, being subjected to an intermediate toughening process prior to being plated. The polishing shop is a scene of activity day and night, -130 polishers working in shifts. Electrically driven dust-extractor Fans keep the air pure, and suck away the unhealthy dust. New Hudson frames, aftet brazing, are scientifically trued, filed up, and given a coating of lacquer preparatory to receiving their four coats of enamel. The lacquer prevents rust, even if the enamel gets chipped in use. Over a hundred hands are kept busy making brakes and brake fittings. Every process is carried out 'with untiring watchfulness and system, whioh ensures the faulty wor detection and rejection of any piece of k. '

div.head: Motor Cycling for Ladies.
div.p: Motor Cycling for Ladies.

- Although a few ladies experimented with motor 'bicycles in the days of Small low-powered engines, it is generally conceded that the modem machines are quite unadapted for use by skirted riders. With a tri-car the case is different, and the recent performance of Miss Muriel Hind, in driving a machine of this type from London to Edinburgh within 24 hours, should do much to direct atten- tion to the possibilities of a tri-car in the hands of a lady.

div.head: Hints about Gas Lamps.
div.p: Hints about Gas Lamps.

It is well not to fill up with carbide more than three-porters of the space available for the pur- pose in an acetylene lamp, as the lime produced by the action of the water swells into a larger bulk. Cases have occurred where the spun metal bolder has been unequal to the pressure. and has burst. Care should also betaken, in charging, that no grains of carbide lodge on the edge of the holder, otherwise, when the lamp is screwed up, and the water turned on, a disconcerting escape of gas may occur, liable to cause alarm on the application elf a liuht.

div.head: Deadly Tramline.
div.p: The Deadly Tramline.

Scarcely a week passes without serious and sometimes fatal accidents occurring to cyclists, owing to skidding on the watered rails of tram- ways. It seems impossible to deter the companies from resorting to watering as a means of lessening friction, although an engineer has pronounced the advantage gained to be negligible. Another source— of danger to wheelmen is the central slot on some of the electrified lines, which becoming enlarged by wear, forms a treacherous opening capable of engulfing a cycle tyre, with serious results. At present cyclists have no remedy against the com- panies.

div.head: Concerning Steps.
div.p: Concerning Steps.

A writer in the a T. C. 'Gazette' complains of the attenuated proportions of the step fitted to some safeties, and points out the danger in the case of a breakage when mounting. Since the general adoption of the free wheel, the step mount 'has been generally abandoned. Mounting by the left pedal, or by throwing the right leg over the saddle, are actions which have become second nature to the great majority of riders, and it is difficult to realize that there can exist any general wish to return to the ancient, ungainly, and un- comfortable method associated with the step.

div.head: CROSFIELD'S RECREATION GROUND. ----- The Opening Ceremony.
div.p: CROSFIELD'S RECREATION GROUND. ----- The Opening Ceremony.

1 Saturday was a red letter day for the employes of Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons Ltd. Under delightful weather conditions a ceremony which had long been looked forward to with pleasure—the open- ing of the new recreation ground in Hood-lane—was witnessed by a great gathering of workpeople. Many townspeople who attended as visitors felt disposed to envy the employes of this progressive firm who, by paying one penny per week to the Recreation Fund, obtain such splendid facilities. The ground is very ' pleasantly and conveniently situated in Hood-lane and could not be better adapted for recreative purposes. It is ten acres in extent and thus affords the most ample accommodation. For many months the work of laying out the land has proceeded, and it is now almost completed, so that the workpeople and their friends— the latter will be admitted at a charge of Id. each—will be able to while away the cool sulnmer evenings in healthy sports. Bowling 1 enthusiasts can indulge in the game to their hearts' content on a well-appointed green and cricketers are also admirably catered for. The ground also com- prizes within its area a cycle track, croquet lawns, hockey and football fields and lawn tennis courts. There is full equipment for the various games, the whole completed by a commodious pavilion. As was explained last week, it is a condition of employment that each person shall contribute one penny per,week to a Recreation Fund. The rule was at first confined to the workpeople and was suggested by them with the view of providing a Recreation Ground for the cricket, football, athletic and bowling_ sections of the old Athletic Club, as well as other means of rational atausement and social and physical recreation. Later, the offices ,and chemical laboratory entered into the scheme. Thus every employ 6 by virture of his con- tribution is a member of the Recreation Club. The fund is controlled by the Works Council, a body repre- sentative of all departments whose functions are in the main advisory but which in this matter acts as trustee in the interest of the workpeople, It was a matter of considerable disappointment flat Mr. A. E. Crosfield, M.P., who had been announced to I open the ground, was prevented by indisposition from 1 attending. The ceremoney was therefore performed Iby Mrs. J. J. Crosfield. A procession was formed at the works, headed by the band and including the fire prigade and ambulance corps, looking very smart in their uniforms. Its progress to Hood-lane was watched by large crowds. Amongst those who were in waiting at the recreation ground were :—Mr. and Mrs. J. 3. Crosfield, Captain G. R. Crosfield, Colonel Kemp ex-MP.( for Heywood), Dr., Mrs. and Miss Markel, Mr. H. Kingdon, Mr. and Mrs. Medley, Mr. Layton, Mrs. C. E. Parker, Dr. and Mrs. Prentice, Mr. ana Mrs. F. Smith, and Mr. and Mrs. F. J. Lord. The opening proceedings were, very brief. Mr. THOMAS KNOWLES said they would be sorry to hear that Mr.A. H.Crosfield, M.P., had telegraphed that owing to ill-health he would be unable to be present. Mrs. J. J. Crosfield had kindly consented to open the ground and he bac) pleasure in asking her to do so. , Dirs. CROSFIELD, standing at the entrance of the pavilion, said : " I have very great pleasure in declaring this recreatioal ground open." Mrs. Crosfield and the other visitors then inspected the pavilion and were much pleased with the arrange- ments.

Several opening games were afterwards played Dr. Markel engaged in a game of bowls With fir.J.Kendrick, while Captain Crosfield, Mr. Medley, Colonel Kemp, and Mr. J. J. Crosfield opened the tennis court. The great attraction was a cricket match—ladies v. gentle- men— wh,ch was most amusing. Mr. J. J. Crosfield bowled the first ball. The men had to play with their left hands and use broom sticks instead of bats and thus handicapped they were beaten by 65 runs to 27. Altogether the afternoon was most enjoyably spent and should prove a happy augury for the success of the recreation ground.

div.head: PADGATE;
div.p: PADGATE;

THE WALKING DAY.—This annual festival is to take place on Saturday, and the procession, which is timed to start at two o'clock, will be made up of scholars from the Church and Wesleyan Sunday schools and the children from the Padgato cottage Homes—the band of the latter institution leading. The route will be down Padgate-lane to the finger post at Orford-road and thence to Fearnhead. After tea at their respective schools the scholars will depart to their fields—the Church and Cottage Homes childrein finding accommoda- tion in a field near the National School and the Wes- leyan children occupying their usual field near the rail- way bridge.
- NATIONAL FREE CEIURCE COUNCIL. NEW DEVELOPMENT.

It has beendeo ided to hold in connection with the National Council of the Evangelical Free Churches a aeries of annual spiritual conventions somewhat on the lines of the Keswick movement but with a broader platform. The first of these Conventions will be held at Harrogate from Sunday August 12th to Sunday August 19th. Among those who have already consented to take part are :—Dr. itendel Harris, Rev. Dr. Horton, Rev. Thomas Law, Rev. H. Elvet Lewis, Rev. F. B. Meyer, 8.A.. and Gipsy Smith. The programme will include early morning prayer meetings, morning devo- tional conferences, afternoon rambles, over tea confer- ences and evening evangelistic services. This convention will be open to all who may wish to attend. No representatives will be appointed. A list of hotels and boarding houses with their tariffs is being prepared,and can be obtained with all information on application to Rev. Thomas Law, Memorial Hall, Farrtngdon-street London, E.G.

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith.
The Aldermanic Vacancy.

Sir,—The duty of selecting candidates for our Municpal Council. is one that requires great thought and consideration on the part of those appointed to %elect same, because after the serious revelations brought to light in the criminal court it is most essential that men of the highest And noblest integrity are brought forward. Men whose patriotism and devo- tion for the welfare of the town is at heart. I do not think it is at all possible to exaggerate our responsi- bility for bearing our part in seeing that we are governed by the right sort of men in our local concerns. Those who are familiar with the agitation of the last few years must know that a very conspicuous place in %hat record must be assigned to the struggles for muni- cipal purity. And whoever shoulders the mantle of the late Alderman Roberts let us hope he will be a gentle- Irian who will maintain the dignity of our municipal Council. Sankey-street, War ring t on.
J. MARSH,

• 336 While we have 17 come from Penketh to Sankey to be educated,onlylsix children go fromSankey to Penketh. The present Council School, which was formerly a Board School and was erected in 1686, has paid an annual sum of £123 for 17 years, and ,CB3 per annum for three years on account of interest and sinking fund,and no outside parish has contributed a single penny towards this, except within the last three years the Lancashire County Council have contributed one quarter of the annual instalment. And yet in the face of this an attempt is being made to compel the ratepayers of Sankey to pay towards the erectionand maintenance of a school in Penketh which will be of no use to the parishioners of Great Sankey, and in which they have no interest whatsoever. As a matter of fact the school which it is proposed to erect is altogether above the requirements of Penketh, although this is a matter which effects them as ratepayers. They propose to erect a school to accommodate 460 children, whereas the present average attendance both at the Wesleyan and Church school is only 266, and this in the face of the fact that the population of Penketh has been stationery for years, and there is no indication of an improvement. The injustice of the effort to make Great Sankey Pay for the erection of schools at Penketh bears doubly hard when we remember that Sankey will have to pay £93 per annum for the next 10 years before the present debt on its own school is paid off. To meet this an average rate of sixpence in the pound has been levied each year and not a penny has been paid by Penketh. And yet we are asked to further tax ourselves in the interest of a parish which has never helped us to the extent of one farthing. As Great Sankey is composed chiefly of the farming class this injustice would be doubly 'raid if it is allowed ,to be carried through. It is only necessary to remem- ber that only six children go to Penketh from Sankey, r while 17come from Penketh to the Sankey schools. This lof itself clearly shows that Sankey will have no use for the proposed new schools, and it behoves the ratepayers of Great Sankey to at once show their opposition to this inequitable scheme, or they will be saddled with an increased rate for which they will get no adequate return. Both the Parish Council and the local school managers are doing everything possible in the interest of the ratepayers, but if we are to be successful we must have the solid backing from the residents and farmers of Great Sankey. A petition is being formu- lated in opposition to this scheme, which it behoves every ratepayer to sign, Yours faithfully, WILLIA:11 YIJRNESS. Fern Lea, Great Sankey. ,
FRED STOTT,

• Death of Mrs. T. G. Rylands. We record with regret the death which took place on Saturday of Mrs. Rylands, widow of the late Mr. Thomas Glazebrooklands, Highfields, Thelwall, She was deeply respected, and her decease is much regretted by a large circle of friends in Thelwall and Warnngton. At one time Mrs. Rylands was well known, taking a great interest in her husband's public work in Warrington, hut since his death she had lived in comparative retirement, having been an invalid for some time past. Mrs. Rylands was Mayoress of War- rington in 1338-0, discharging the duties of the office with great grace. The body of the deceased lady was cremated at the Manchester Crematorium on Tuesday. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. Geo. Feather, of Glazebury. The mourners at the Crematorium were :—Mr. Paul Rylands, Mr. W. Harry Rylands, Mr. G. P. Mason, Mr. Gordon Rylands, Mr. W. Peter Rylands, Mr. J. J. Bleckly, Mr. L. W. Reynolds, Mr. J. C. Bromfield. Floral tributes were sent by the following :—Mr. and Mrs. Paul Rylands, "Ralph, Geoffrey, Dorothy and Marjorie," Miss G. Rylands, Mr. W. Harry Rylands, Mr. J. Wilson RookeVr. and Mrs. Bairstow, Mrs. Peter Rylands, Miss Morris, the , servants at Highfields, Mrs. Hobson and Mrs. Dewhurst, Mrs. P. H. Newnham, Miss Blanche Rylands, Mr. and Mrs.. Peter Rylands, Miss Maud Bleckly, Mr. and Mrs. Bleckly, Miss Raynes and Nurse Blancowe. The whole of the funeral arrangements were carried out by Mr. Ralph Johnson, Bridge-street, Warrington.

div.head: 10, Battersby-lane. Trades Unionism in the Painting Trade.
div.p: 10, Battersby-lane. Trades Unionism in the Painting Trade.

Sir,—ln your issue of the 16th appears a letter from Mr. W. J. Pearce, in which he denounces Trade Unionism in the painting trade. Mr. Pearce is well- known as a designer, but we have yet to learn that he is an authority on the history of trade unionism, and one wonders if the Manchester educational authorities have added the attacking of trade unionism t", Mr. Pearce's other duties. Mr. Pearce approaches the ques- tion of employment from a wrong basis, and gets astray in his argument. He says "the result (of unionism) has been to throw out of employment a large and increasing number of men." Does Mr. Pearce think that if wages were on a sliding scale the public would find more work, and so keep the men fully employed? He should know very well this would not be so. Paint- ing is done because it requires doing, and not for the purpose of keeping man employed. Therefore union or no union, the average quantity of work coming into the trade would remain as at pre- sent. What the unions aim at is to secure for their members the best conditions possible, while doing that work, and to assist their more aril° rtunate members. Our Trade Society paid £35,302 in benefits last year. Mr. Pearce's picture of the sliding scale is very pretty but very old, we have met with it before when trying to improve our conditions of labour. He gives as an instance a shop when the wages before trade unionism were" .£3 to 225." He does not state how many men received the .C 3 but we can imagine the proportions. "The wages now paid are from 455. to 35s."—a very strong case for trade unionism. This is what the Union exists for—the good of the greatest number. Mr. Pearce says that workmanship has deteriorated and gives as an instance signwriting and stencilling which he says is now accomplished by boys and girls. I hope Mr. Pearce's technique is better than his logic, he is not fortunate in his illustrations. As an answer to this I may state that some few years since the oldest master painter in this town (since deceased) was asked : Was it not a fact that the average painter of to-day was a more respect- able, a more reliable, and a more efficient workman than the painters of fifty years ago? His answer was "Certainly he is." I think this gentleman's practical experience of a long lifetime counts before Mr. Pearce's theory. If the Unions can (and they have) improve the conditions of the average man, they may safely leave the Heaven-sent genius "at ,C 3 per week "to look after himself. He is rare. I have never yet met with him. What our trade requires is not less trade unionism but more of it. Our trade is crippled by masters who, to make more profit, or to undercut other masters, fill their shops with lads and so crowd the trade, that men cannot make a decent living at it, and until this is stopped, to quote Mr. Pearce " The per- centage of unemployed will undoubtedly increase until the workers deliver themselves from this new form of bondage."

div.head: TRADE UNIONIST PAINTER.
div.p: A TRADE UNIONIST PAINTER.
A Plea for a Proper Holiday.
A .
K

Sir,—l would be obliged to you for a little of your 'valuable space for the purpose of ventilating a quesiton which of late years especially, has appealed to me in a very strong sense and that is—the holiday question. It seems to me, we are far from enjoying a real holi- day and, the purpose for whrch a holiday should be devoted ; simply because we have too many. I take it for granted that holidays are for rest, and rational enjoyment, that our mental, physical and vital powers may be recuperated; and which under the present stress and strain and strenuous effort of business life the body so greatly needs. But I fail to see how this is or can be obtained under a system of holiday taking which may be best associated by the term " fit and start." Si.ow, in the first place this sort of holiday cannot in the very nature of things be regarded as beneficial, therefore not ideal. Here we are frittering our lives away, a day now and another Ina few weeks or a month or two hence. Commence say with New Year Day, for example, which is pretty generally absurd, we pass on to Good Friday, to be followed two days later with Easter Monday, next we have Whit Monday—just passed—a week hence is the Town's special ; designated, Walking 1 Day ; close upon its heels there comes August Bank I Holiday and finally after about four months we arrive I at Christmas Day and Boxing Day. Thus, we have, -something like eight days holiday per annum scattered I promisciously over a whole year in a fashion that might I 'suggest they had been dropped by some thunderbolt ' from the heavens and had fallen in such an limns poet's fashion, that nobody can be fairly said to derive benefit by any one of them. Now, sir, I wonld suggest—as a worker of the strenu- ous kind—that something more real and tangible than a mere Bank Holiday or street procession be given, for after all many of these holidays, especially the Walking Day is more of a business upset than a profit, and no careful and candid observer of the social and pecuniary aspect of that day, cannot have failed to see that any immediate gain to a business is lost in the stagnation that takes place immediately after. I need not enter into the dislocation of traffic in the streets and special police arrangements, these are open to all observers of the most careless and casual. To shop assistants ; especially, most if not all of these holidays are, in their ; mildest forms a curse, inasmuch as they \ bring no pleasure at all to their lives, and in all cases have been ; more than earned by the Arduous and vexatious toil and ssertion of the previous week., I would not deny these or any other workers their trip to Blackpool,Southport, the Lakes, ttc., but, on the contrary, instead of a solitary wearying day—or probably kit a few hours-- at one of these places my idea is that they should be I given an entire week. Now suppose that some of ' these Bank holidays were dropped entirely, and a week or ten days substituted and, granted that this general holiday could be arranged; say, to commence about the August Bank Holiday or at such a time as pear that season as convenient ; and further, I would suggest I that this much looked-forward-to-day, Walking Day. he , held the Friday previous to the August Bank Holiday; there would thus then commence is worker's complete week of rest while it would in all probability so far as the day school children are concerned be included in I their summer holidays. Such a holiday I can conceive I being acceptable to all. A system of this kind does , obtain in the busy towns of North-East Lancashire. I Burnley for instance, Colne Nelson and other East Lan- I cashire towns close all their works for a weeks holiday in July. And at this season tens of thousands of mill and factory hands may be seen in their holiday attire , leaving their honies for the quiet and seclusion of some I of the North of England valleys; there to regale themselves with the sweet fresh air, and the rich I but substantial fare of some farm house, and then to I returo fresh and invigorated and ready for the toils of anoth'u• year. As to the pecuniary side of this question it is explained by the fact, that every works has its,
, t

holiday club, and there is no earthly reason why such a system could not be inaugurated in this town. It should not be a difficult matter for a strong committee of works' managers, foremen and secretaries of the various worker's unions to arrange a meeting and out- line an holiday after the manner indicated, the utility lof which can not be over-rated. As at preseat con- stituted holidays are expensive, irksome and to not a few, even disastrous ; while to all, a loss, or what may not improperly be described as a waste of money. excepting of course the inevitable. trippers' caterers, railway, steamboat and other companies. But the day tripper returns after his long railway or other journey of anywhere from six to twenty hours completely fagged out, and who will deny that this kind is anything but a holiday, but on the contrary a hard days' work. These may be matters to take into consideration which are of a local character and, which will undoubtedly need to be studied carefully, but granted intelligent action and application I can't think that anything would be beyond the wit and wisdom of thoughtful men to devise. In conclusion what is sought is not less holi- days, but rather, as much if not more than at present with this difference—that this willy nilly, puff and dart holiday making be brought to an end and, give every possible chance to every class of toilers the privilege of a clear week per annum in the hope that they may enjoy a proper rest and return refreshed and invigorated for another year's toil.—l am, truly yours, T. A. Mac FLEET, Latchford, 19th 1906.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, June 23, 1906.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, June 23, 1906.

themselves to wipe off the arrears and a victory by Fielding over Rogers of 15-1 levelled matters up a little. W. Ashcroft further reduced the Pearson and Knowles lead and T. Percival brought the teams within two points of each other. It appeared as though Richmond's were fated to be behind as Pemberton lost by the odd point after leading throughout in his game with D. Ferguson. P. Hankinson however stepped into the breach and his efforts being ably supported by T. Jones Richmonds for the first time rejoiced in a lead. Then were their hopes once more dashed to the ground as Kenwright defeated NV. Lee by 10 points and P. and K. claimed the advantage. Richmonds were not to be denied and E. Fletcher and R. Bennett both winning' handsomely P. and K. when play ceased were in arrear to the extent of 15 points. Theactualviotory for Richmonds was one of 30 points as one P. and K. player failed to put in an appearance and T. Cooper was given a walk over.
To-day's matches are Fletcher's (No. 1) v. Warrington Wire Rope Orford Tannery v. Rylands (No. 1) and Forshaws v. Whitecross (No. 2), Refere?, N. Cook.

Cycling. By no-one has the spell of summer weather been more heartily welcomed than by the cyclists who have, of course, availed themselves of the opportunity of visit- ing their favourite resorts. There was a splendid muster of members of the Warrington Cycling Club on Satur- day for the run to Oulton Park. The country side was looking at its best and the spin through DelAmere Forest was thoroughly enjoyed. Tea was served at the Egerton Arms and afterwards the party, by special per- mission, visited the pretty grounds of Sir Philip Grey Egerton. This part of the programme was highly appreciated and pleasant recollections of the visit will long be retained. On the return journey a halt was called at Little Leigh where a couple of hours were spent in a convivial way.

On Tuesday evening the weather was again beauti- fully fine and the run to the quaint old village of War- burton attracted a large turnout. Several games of bowls werlo played on the Saracen's Head green and, after a brief musical programme, the return journey was pleasantly accomplished in good time.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket,

Warrington still head the West Lancashire League but if they want to retain that proud position they will have to shape better than they -did in their match with Earlestown on Saturday. The previous week the Warringtonians had shown such excellent form that ardent supporters believed they were going to carry all before them, but there's many a slip—and the eleven experienced a rebuff at Earlestown where their opponents secured a majority of 25. Neither side was in particularly good scoring form—the wicket did not favour the batsmen—but the home eleven showed just sufncient superiority to gain the victory. J. Callon made the best stand for the visitors. He hit out freely and scored with a rapidity which was quite refreshing. He had the satisfaction of carrying out his bat for 22. The next best scorer was W. V. Turton who made 16,whi le A. Thewlis was responsible for 14. The bowling for the Earlestown side was shared mainly by Bates and Warburton who accotinted for 4 wickets for 57 runs and 3 for 15 respectively.

For Earlestoma T. Marsh did the best service with the bat. By dint of very careful cricket he ran up 35 before he was smartly caught by ,Duckworth. His brother also made a useful stand, his innings realizing 16. Of the Warrington bowlers, Bibby was very effective taking 4 wickets for 35 runs. Cresswell also gave the home batsmen considerable trouble and captured 3 wickets at a cost of 32 runs.

While the senior eleven fared badly, the second eleven had quite the best of the argument with their Earlestown visitors to whonalthey administered a particularly severe drubbing. The majority for the Warringtonians was no less than 129, the top scorer being R. G. Pierpoint whose 61 included nine fours and three threes. H Callon wrought great havoc with the ball, his capture being six wickets for 22 runs. We were rather sur- prised to find that he was not included in the first eleven, as he has been bowling uncommonly well this 11 season. Bennett also did splendid work in the bowling department, securing four wickets for 41 runs.
Prescot t present head the second division, with Warrington one point behind.

Sankey Wire Mills visited Moore but failed to account for the villagers, an interesting game resulting in a victory for Moore and Daresbury by 15. A. Dutton (26) and the Rev. T. T. Lee Jones (15) hatted in fine style for the winners and H. Taylor bowled splendidly, taking four wickets for 23 runs. For the Wire Mills, Partridge and J. Hawthorn gave creditable displays for their respective totals of 20 and 13, the first-named being at the wicket nearly an hour. H. Brough was to the fore with the bowling and took seven wickets. At the close of the game an enjoyable time was spent at the Moore Institute where the teams were entertained by Mr. Ernest Houghton, president of the Wire Mills Club.
The victorious career of the Bewsey Wesleyans was checked on Saturday by St. Paul's who had little diffi- culty in running up a margin of 4S. S. Mason (17) and W. Lawless (14) were the top scorers.
Stretton and Appleton beat the Mersey Club,a feature of the game being the bowling of Ratcliffe who took 6 wickets for 21 runs. Jones batted in vigorous style for his 23.

Penketh entertained Widnes White Rose and triumphed by a 35 majority. Ward's sound batting conk tributed largely to the success of the villagers, his innings realizing 41. Shoobridge's deliveries were practically unplayable and his average worked out at under three runs each for the six wickets he took.

The Works Competition continues to arouse great interest and next week the second round will be entered upon. On Tuesday evening Walker's met Newall's whom they defeated by 66. W. Baird (29.), was the most successful batsman and Dargan bowled brilliantly, taking eight wickets for five runs. He is a splendid bowler, as many other teams have discovered to their cost.

div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

The first round in connection with the Lancashire and Cheshire individual merit competition was com,menced on Saturday and attracted a large crowd to the Lord Nelson Hotel, Urmston. G. Ball, (Warrington), and W. Cartwright (Gorton), were the first players to meet and the Gorton man was quickly left behind Ball run- ning to 9-1. With the score at 12-15 Cartwright had a chance but he failed to score again and was beaten by 21-12. F. Millar and J. A. Harrison had little trouble in qualifying for the second round defeating respectively W. 'E. Harrison, cud F. Bamford. T. Humphreys . beat S. Brooks, Prestwich by good bowling by 21-11. One of the surprises of the afternoon was the defeat by W. Hampson, of T. Ellison. The Warrington man went to the front 64, and then fell off surprisingly. Harrison secured the block and with three good runs ran from 1-6 to 11-6 and from 11-7 to 16-7, Ellison scored three and then had to retire completely beaten. Joseph Allison, a ona time champion and the popular proprietor of the Cemetery green still retains his old form but it looked very bad for him when E. Whitley, ' Winnington, was 13-4 and 17-10. A useful run of eight however gave him the lead and he ran out winner 21-19. Another Cemetery player A. Scott had a long fight with A. Morgan of Gorton.Starting badly Scott was 9-13 when he carried the game to 17-13. At 18 the players peeled but from this point Scott got home 21-13. A. Gleave is an unusually promising young player and was pitted against J. Grundy of Leigh Railway, the 1904 champion. After an indifferent start Gleave went to the front and won 21-18,

The path of the Warrington and District Bowling League is by no means smooth. At the commencement of the season a proposal was made, which, had it been accepted and acted upon by the clubs in the district, would have made the competition the most interesting in the district. It was that the radius of the League's activity should be extended to five miles and that the tournament should be conducted on the knock out principle, on paper the suggestion is a sound and i sensible one but actually carried out t has proved a dismal failure and has resulted in the abandonment of the League programme for this year. Six clubs only signified their intention of competing for championship honours and with so small an entry it was suggested that the competitions should be conducted on League lines as in the past with home and away matches. So enamoured however were the League Committee of the knock-out 1 principle that they adhered to it. Difficulties were at once experienced in the way of inducing clubs to com- plete their matches as all interest had apparently been i lost and failing to make a start t was on Wednesday night decided to abandon the programme. It is to be hoped that this fate will not result in the disbandoning of the League but that nest season it will again take its proper place in local bowling circles.

Whilst the League has, for the-time being had to suspend operations the works competitions tlourisheth exceedingly, and this week end will witness the con- clusion of the first round after an excellent series of matches. After a week's rest play was resumed last Saturday on the " Bowling Green" green and close finishes were witnessed. The only match which did not I rouse the spectators to enthusiasm was the one between Artingstall and Monks Hall (No. 1) as the bruslunakers from the first never had a chance. S. Massey started by clean plating J. Tunstall whilst J. Deakin and T.R ighy were very little behind both allow- ing their opponents to score only one point. It seemed as though nothing could stay the progress of the Monks Hall men and R. Walsh falling an easy victim to W. Hatton the forgemen led by 55 points with four men off the green. Their position continued to improve and two games later they were 75 ahead. The remainder of the points were more evenly divided and at the close the victors had only increased their lead to SG.

-- A far different state of things was seen when Rylands (no. 4) and St. Helens teams were associated. B. Maguire and J. Harrison were tho first to meet and after leading 8-0 and 12-3, Nlaguire won 1.5-6. The next game also went to Rylands, S. Sheldon winning by the odd point. Starting well Sheldon went to 9-1 when his opponent got in a good run and came to 10-9. The two peeled at 11 when Crossland went to the front 14-11 only to be beaten in the end. A win for St. Helens raised their hopes and when J. Barrow defeated J. James 15-8 the total scores were brought equal. R. Illidge carried Rylands to the front when W. Allen did the same for St. Helens and for a time the position of the two teams was constantly charging.

For a time R. Harrison put up a good fight against Barnes but falling off towards the close the teams again drew level. J. Heywood and R. Smith had a long tight and each led at the various stages for Heywood in the end to give St. Helens the advantage by one point. Visions of a true sporting finish were in the air and each wood was watched with the closest attention. To the dismay of his comrades J. Clarice WAS unable to guage C. lover and as he went down 3-la the St. Helens prospect's were somewhat dimmed, only to be made worse by E. Poole. T. Tweedle buoyed up their hopes and defeating J. Meakin 15-7 gave Rylands the task of scoring six in order to claim the match. J. Wilkes and G. Berry wore the last pair to meet and starting with a double Wilkes made the match more uncertain. Berry replied with a single and then getting five woods home in succession practically ended the match and Rylands qualified for the second round.

After a bad start Richmonds succeeded in defeating Pearson and Knowles (No 2) team by a comfortable margin. J. Smith opened the match with W. Eyes and lost 1-15. W. Floyd improved very little upon his colleagues score and after his game with Stockton Pearson and Konwles led by 21points. Richmoads set

div.head: Swimming.
div.p: Swimming.

The first round of the Warrington Works squadron championship was continued on Thursday before a good attendance at the Warrington batih. The first teams to race were P. and K. and Post Office (N 0.1. team. P. and K. at once took the lead and gained half a length which they kept throughout. Corporation were awarded a walk over their opponents, P. Walker and Sons, not putting in an appearance. Swimming againsta scratch team they were beaten by a touch. Monks Hail and Post Office (No. 2.) teams had a good fight which • Monks Hall won byhalf a length. Co-operative recea d theirquietus from Crosfields.

Later in the evening the Warrington polo team met a team from Salford in the first round of the Lancashire and Cheshire Cup competition. Warrington who were not at full strength in the first :half defended tie shallow end and Woods was called upoi to save a hard sbot from Whitehead. A minute later Wood saved a shot from E. Forsyth at the expense of scorner. A penalty was given against Salford in the goal mouth and obtaining possession Pemberton scored. Ashton increased the lead a minute later with a shot from the Warrington quarter line, and half-time arrived with Warrington leading by two goals to nil. Re-starting a had pass by Pemberton gave Forsyth an opening from which he easily scored. Ashton sent in several long shots but Swann was able to keen his goal clear. Forsyth equalized a little later. The game was very hotly contested and there was little to choose between the teams. Woods was putting in some splendid work but when Rallantyne got the ball a few yards from the , posts he had no chance and Salford went to the front. 1 Final :—Salford, 3 goals ; Warrington, 2 goals.

div.head: iingiing
div.p: iingiing

A correspondent writes to say that with reference to the fishing on the Almere Farm, Eaton Estate I visited that place on Whit-Sunday and saw Mr. Williams the tenant who informed me that the charges for fishing the Dee at that point were as follows :—for one day a charge of 3d. is made,and not a shilling as was rumoured whilst for a party camping no charge is made except the ground rent Is. per day.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO MR. JOHN UPSON. Illuminated Address from the ' Teachers' Association.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO MR. JOHN UPSON. Illuminated Address from the ' Teachers' Association.
A largely attended meetinr of the Warrington and District Teachers' Association washeld in the Technical School on Tuesday evening. Mr. John Upson presided over a very representative gathering. _

div.head: HALF-YEARLY REFORM.
div.p: HALF-YEARLY REFORM.

On the question of half-yearly reports being required by the Education Committee from the bead teachers on the work of the assistant class teachers, the reply received from the Director, Mr. J. Moore Murray, was not considered to be altogether to the liking of the teachers concerned, and it was decided, after consider- able discussion, that the School Management Com- mittee be asked to receive a deputation upon the matter of confidential reports on the work of class teachers in the borough.

div.head: PRESENTITION TO MR. UPSON.
div.p: PRESENTITION TO MR. UPSON.

- A presentation of an illuminated address was then made to Mr. John (Srpson on his retirement from the position of secretary of the association which he had held for the past six years. The address reads : " National Union of Teachers. Warrington Branch. To Mr. John UPson. The executive of the National Union of Teachers and your fellow members of the Warrington Teachers' Association desire, on the occasion of your retirement from the post of secre- tary of that Association, to record their high appreci- tion of the valuable services which you have rendered to the cause of education and the educator. During your six years' terms of office in the associa- tion your devoted and successful labours have abundantly tleserved the honourable recognition which we hereby desire to convey, and in asking you to accept this expression of esteem and gratitude the executive and the association earnestly wish you health, happiness and Godspeed. Signed on behalf of the excutive of the National Union of Teachers, T. P. Sykes. president; J. H. Yoxall, general secretary. Signed on behalf of the local association, Sydney W.Jeffer, president ; Frank EL Longshaw, secretary. Russell-square, London, 1206." Mr.,JOUN CANN, headmaster of the Orford Schools, made the presentation and said that he, as one of the oldest members of the Warrington Branch of the National Union of Teachers, had great pleasure in doing so. He had known Mr. Upson for many years, and had observed carefully his method of work, and he must say that he had exhibited tact, judgment and a careful handling of any case with which he had had to deal. His work generally on behalf of elementary teachers was worthy of the highest eulogy. (Applause.) „ Mr. E. WALLINGTON also said he war pleased to have I that opportunity of paying some tribute to Mr. Upson's work, and he had had during the past few years some chance of observing what he had accomplished for education. (Applause). Mr. Upson had attended faith- fully to his duties. Fie had had little time at home. He was Forry that Mrs. Upson was absent on that occasion , and that she was not able to share somewhat in her husband's pleasure. The local branch of the N.U.T. was indebted to Mr. Upson for years of real hard work, much of which woe of a private character, but such had been the tact ' and judgment which the late secre- tary had exhibited that litigation had been avoided. (Applause.) He hoped that Mr. Upson would live long to read that beautiful address,and that it would impress upon him the high esteem with which the teachers of Warrington regarded his work. Mr. STANSFIELD said he esteemed Mr. Upson's work,' and he was sure that every teacher present would admit that Mr. Upson had proved an efficient and practical secretary. (Hear, hear). He further hoped that he would aspire to the highest office of the Union for it was certain that he would receive a large measure of support from all elementary teachers of the country. (Applause.) Mr. JEFFERY spoke of the successful work which Mr, Upson had accomplished in the cause of education in Warrington. Mr. UPSON, in reply, said that on this occasion he found it difficult to express his feelings. He was grateful however for the honour which his fellow teachers had seen fit to confer upon him in presenting him with that illuminated testimonial. Lie had not laboured for reward, but he assured them that he would value the address as one of his choicest 1 possessions, as being an appreciation of the work he had done. He had now been 21 years in Warrington, ' and during the whole of that time he ha at been a member of the Union and engaged in its 0E14%1 work, I but like work of this particular character the results did not appear on the surface. The clerical I work had been large, and as secretary he had been a I sort of " guide, philosopher and friend " to teachers I generally. He hoped that whatever had been ! his actions in any official capacity no resent- ment had been caused. Publicly he took pleasure in this class of work, and liked to be in the forefront of the battle, and bear the burden when any was to be borne. As a member of the Education Committee his first consideration had been, not the teacher, but the child, and he was not primarily the teachers' representative, but one of those who desired to advance the cause of education, and secondly the cause of teachers. He had had a good working com- mittee of teachers in connection with the work of the N.U.T. ideally, but still there might be more active workers than there were at the present time, and not so many who were content to rest upon the work of others. (Hear, hear). He was pleased to know that the question of presenting him with that testimtrnial, however, had been taken up so enthusiasti- cally, and he believed that it had not been given because it was the proper thing to do, but was really an appre- ciation of his work and his efforts. (Applause). It was decided that the next meeting take the form of a picnic. Several new members were proposed.
