till death. He would be much missed. He (the Vicar) would miss him very ranch. The late Alderman Roberts was not a man to make a great profession, but he loved the House of God, and he must have loved his God. But he had only vacated his seat here below to take his seat in God's court above. The hymn "On the resur- rection morning" was sung, and the organist having played the Dead March in "Saul," the service vms brought to a conclusion. CONSERVATIVE TRIBUTES.

.peaking at a garden party given to the Junior Con- servative Association by Mr. and Mrs. Roger C. Parr at Grappenhall Hayes on Saturday, Mr. ROBERT PIER- POINT said he c,4uld not but think that that was to many of them a day in which gloom was to a certain extent mixed up with their gaiety, and it would ill befit them, and especially hithself, if he were to address them on that the first public opportunity he had had without expressing feelings of sorrow in having lost one of their best friends in the person of the late Alderman John Roberts. (Hear. hear.) He did not think that there were many in that assembly who had a greater right to speak of Alderman Roberts—he preferred to call him by his familiar name, John Roberts—than he had, as he had been connected with him for 25 or 30 years, and he could assure them that the more he was connected with him the more he had learnt to respect him. (Applause). Mr. Roberts was one of the staunchest and best of men, who never spared himself, and was always ready at the call of his party. He was a thorough-going hard fighter, but he did not think that even in the opposing ranks he had one single enemy. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BENNETT, also added his tribute. He could not help thinking of the genial and kindly figure whom they all loved and so affectionately remembered, who, in the ordinary course of things would have been with them that day. He could hardly realize that Alderman Roberts was no longer with them, especially when he remembered that only a week ago he was speaking to the Conservative Associa- tion in the courageous spirit he usually displayed, and telling them how much, in spite of the present dis- couragements, he was going to" buck up," to use his own phrase, and make a good fight for the cause he had so much at heart. They all respected and honoured his memory, and they were sorry he was not able ;4) be with them that day, as he had been on so many oo asions of a similar character.

div.head: LATE ALDERMAN JOHN ROBERTS.
div.p: THE LATE ALDERMAN JOHN ROBERTS.
Funeral at Warrington Cemetery.

The funeral of the late Alderman Jahn Roberts, , which took place ht the Warrington Cemetery on Saturday, was the occasion of an impressive demonstra- tion of respect. The last rites were witnessed by an exceptionally large gathering, and the representation of numerous public bodies afforded testimony to the active part which the deceased had taken in local . affairs. The members of the Corporation assembled at the Town Hall and joined the cortege at the ; deceased's late residence, 10, Winvvick-road. The ' first part of the burial service was conducted at St- Peter's Church, where the late alderman had been such an enthusiastic and devoted worker from I its foundation. The altar and pulpit were I draped in black, and the service was deeply impressive. The, choir was in attendance, and ' chanted Psalm xc. The hymn "Now the labourer's task is o'er " was also feelingly sung. Mr. Ernest Wilkes presided at the organ. The officiating clergy were the Rev. B. Percival (vicar),the Rev. Henry Russell (cuxate), and the Rev. D. R. James (late curate, and now of Wellington). As the mourners left the church Mr. Wilkes played the "Dead March "in " Saul." Many spectators had assembled along the route to the Cemetery and on every hand were heard expressions of the universal esteem in which the deceased was held. The procession was headed by a detachment of police under the direction of Chief Inspector Phillips and the members of the Connell and magistrates followed. The coffin and hearse were covered with beautiful wreaths and other floral tributes were conveyed in an open carriage. The last rites at the grave side were very brief, the committal sentences being read by the Rev. B. Percival. .

Amongst those present were the following:— Chief Mourners.—Messrs. William John Roberts and Harry Roberts (sons), H. Roberts (brother), T. S. Forster, IV. Rogers, S., T. Wadsworth, J. H. J. Hamp- son, R. Shackleton, A. Jolley, W. J. Shaw, J. Taylor, T. Reddish, F .Neild, H. Collin, T. E. Sangster and F. J. , Dell (all 1250) ; Bro. C. MEMORIAL SERVICE AT ST. PETER'S CHURCH. On Sunday morning a memorial service was held in St. Peter's Church, and was largely attended. Mr. F. Webster was at the organ, and the lessons were read by Mr. T. S. Steel. The hymns sung were "Let saints on earth in concert sing" and" Days and moments quickly flying." The preacher was the Rev. B. Percival, who took for his text the words "Thou shalt be missed because thy seat will be empty." He said their deceased friend worshipped in that church morning and evening. He NNW not a" oncer "if he was able to come at all. The weather bad nothing whatever to do with his coming to church, and it mattered not whether it was hot or cold, whether the sun was shining or whether snow was fall. I lug. It was only because of indisposition, or the fact that he was not at horse that his seat was vacant. They were all aware of the busy, strenuous life he lived, and that the business with which he was connected was to-day a monument of his indefatigable energy ; I also of the important positions he filled in pubiic affairs, with his characteristic energy and success. But the one position in which his name would be handed down to time immemorial would be that of church- warden of St. Peter's Church for the past quarter of a century. He loved the church, and every brick and stone was dear to him. How he loved to tell its story over and over again, from the collecting of the first few pounds to the raising of £5,000, and from the laying of the foundation stone to the completion of the building ! He was inter- ested in every organiz..tion of the church. How generous he was, according to his means, and as those dead remains were being taken through the streets of that poor parish, how reverently and orderly did the poor people stand along the line of route to see the procession. "Thou shalt be missed because thy seat will be empty." What a sterling character he repre- sented. How he loved to do a good and kind act. What inspiration for their young men had they in their deceased friend. They would tire of football, cricket, and all the other gamesbut the pleasure of doing good would remain with them unto the last. It was the only thing that would remain when he (the preacher),and the congregation had done with that parish. Honest John," indeed, in word and deed, faithful and true

div.head: EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
Business of the Next Meeting.
The monthly meeting of the Education Committee will be held at the Town Hall on Monday evening, when the following amongst other business will be con- sidered :

SCHOOL KEEPERS SALARIES. On the recommendation of the Sub-Committee apppointed to consider the question of the payment of school keepers, it was resolved by the Finance Com- mittee (a) that, in view of the probable impending changes in the regulations of the Board of Education governing the accommodation recognised by them in the public elementary schools, it is undesirable at present to make any change in the Committee's rules for the work and remuneration of school keepers ; and (b) that it be made a regulation that no married women be appointed as school-keepers.—ln view of the fore- going resolution, it was further resolved (a) that the temporary engagement of Mrs. Ruth Forster (ne4 Blenkinsop) as school-keeper of the Ladies' School of Industry be continued, from the 16th April, 1903, until such time as her successor is appointed, at a salary at the rate of £52 per annum; and (b) that the Director be instructed to confer v9lith the managers of the Ladies' School of Industry in reference to the appointment of a sohool-keeper for the school.

div.head: SEC-ONDARY SCHOOL BOOK-KEEPING,
div.p: SEC-ONDARY SCHOOL BOOK-KEEPING,

At a meeting of the School Management Committee a letter was read from the Headmaster of the Secondary School and Technical Institute, in explanation of the report upon the keeping of the various stock books at that school, and it was resolved that the explanatibn be received, and that the Director be instructed to com- municate With the Headmaster expressing the com- mittee's hope that this part of his duty will, in the future, receive his most careful attention, and that there will be no further need for complaint in this connection. THE POSITION OF TILE GRAMMAR SCHOOL.

A letter was submitted at the meeting of the School Management Committee from the Board of Education, forwarding copies of an amended draft of the proposed order and scheme for the government of the Warrington Grammar school. It was resolved that a sub-committee, consisting of Mr. Councillor J. Fulton Smith, Mr. Councillor Wilkinson, Mr. John Upson and the Chair- man of the Committee (Rev. Canon Stevenson), ,be appointed to consider the same and to report thereon to the committee. _

A letter from the Board of Education—for Warding copy of a notice in reference to the proposed leasing of land in Tyldesley by the Governors of the Warrin---m Grammar school—was submitted, and the 13,- instructed to intimate in reply that the no objection or suggestion to make in r _ matter. A scheme showing the proposed conditions for the award of the Council scholarships tenable at the War- rington Grammar school,in accordance with the arrange- ment made with the Governors was referred to the sub- committee already appointed to consider the amended Draft Order and Scheme for the government of that school.

SCHOOL CHILDREN AND THE BATHS. At a meeting of the School Management Committee a letter was read from the Town Clerk—intimating that the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee could not see their way to accede to the Committee's request to allow arrangements to be made with the keeper of the Baths to instruct boys from the public elementary school in the Borough in the art of swimming, and it was resolved that the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Com- mittee be approached with a view to their sanction being obtained to the employment by the Education Committee of an instructor for this purpose. xiNG's SCHOLARSHIP EXAMINATIONS. Number of Warrington students accepted for admission to training Colleges, 18 out of 54 examined in 1904, 5 out of 23 examined in 1905 and 15 out of 23 examined in 1906. In view of the unsatisfactory nature of the result, it was decided to invite the Head Master of the Secondary school to furnish the Committee with any comments he may have to make thereon. It was further resolved that the director be instructed to report upon the whole of the organization of the teach- ing staff at the Secondary School and Technical Institute.

ART EXHTBITION. At a meeting of the School Management Committee a letter was submitted from the headmaster of the School of Art suggesting that application should he made to the Board of Education for an exhibition to be held in Warrington of some of the drawinggdarepared in different parts of the country for the National Com- petition and it was resolved that the suggestion be approvecl,and that authority be given for the Board of Education to be approached with a view to such an ex- hibition being held, provided the cost in connection therewith does not exceed the sum of ,ElO. STUDENTS FEES RET UR4E D. A letter was read at a meeting of the School ilranage- inept Committee frbm two students at the Technical Instit!lte last session—complaining of the arrangements made at that school for the class in Metallurgy (Stage II.), and asking, in view of the failure to provide adequate apparatus for the conduct of the class and the taking of the examination, that the fees paid by them should be returned—having been considered, it was resolved that their application be acceded to and that their fees be returned to them.

ALDERMAN BENNETT AND NATIONAL DITTY. At a meeting of the School Management Committee a letter from Mr. Alderman Arthur Bennett—offering a prize of one guinea (to be divided equally between the boys and girls) for the best essay on some phase of national duty by scholars at ths Secondary school— was received, and it was resolTed that the offer be accepted with thanks.

div.head: CLOSING OF SCHOOLS.
div.p: CLOSING OF SCHOOLS.

A report of the Rota Sub-Committee that permission had been given for the St. Alban's, St. Benedict's, St. Mary's, Sacred Heart and Latchford R.C. schools to be closed on Thursday, the 11th June, that day being a day of religious observance, it was resolved by the School Attendance Committee that the action of the Rota Committee be approved. The Rota Committee further reported that they had refused an application received from the Honorary Secretary of the Police Athletic Sports, for the closure of the schools in the Borough on the afternoon of Thursday, the .23rd August, and their action in the matter was approved. A letter was submitted at a meeting of the School Attendance Committee from the managers of the Trinity National school, asking that the Mixed department of that school might be closed on the afternoon of Friday, the 20th July, in order that the scholars' annual picnic might be held that afternoon, but it was resolved that the request be not acceded to.

Festival at Beeston Castle. Favoured with beautiful weather the festival held amid the picturesque ruins of Beeston Castle on Tuesday and Wednesday attracted visitors from all parts of Cheshire and Lancashire. For sixty-three years the festival has been held, and during that period has realised large sums for charities. Of late years, however, the committee find they have no surplus and so they have decided to close, owing to the fact that there are too many functions of a similar character held in the county. The final festival proved most 'enjoyable, the Over Silver Band being in attendance and playing a capital selection of music. The tents and other appliances used were sold by auction at the close of the fete on Thursday.
Nine hundred and nine bodies have now been recovered from the Courrieres mines in North France. 193 men are still missing.

they eriw more of the, works of ninn than of the woi of God, and yet they i e 'lgh amongst tlat shadowed streets to assure them that God was actualll at work upon the face of nature. Their parks and little gardens were not only refreshing to the sight but a ieY to the devout spirit. And when they made their escape from the towns and looked forth upon the panorrna of loveliness which was stretched around them, the eye was keener to observe its beauties on account of the dark surroundings in the midst of which they were usually placed. Further, it was possible for them to rejoice in God as they found Him in His Word. He spoke to them in naturBp. but they came into closer contact with Him in His Holy Book. To some the Bible had been a kind of lesson book, and it was much to be hoped that whatever might happen to it in the course of present controversies, it might not be degraded to the position of a mere lesson book. To many it had been a kind of religious task book, so that people had not learnt to look upon it as a book for pleasure. Yet it was true that some of the highest joys upon earth were to be drawn from contact with God in His Word. Viewed simply as literature, the Word of God came to them in a form of marvellous interest. Even if it were nothing but a book, it was the most interesting book they ha fi any knowledge of. But the human interest of the Scriptures, was the least part of their charm. That was a grand saying of the minister of the men of the " Mayflower" :—" God has yet more light and truth to break forth from his Holy Word." The Puritans saw things in the-Word of God that had never been seen until their time, and still new light had ,been breaking forth from year to year ever since,and it broke forth still in the eyes of the patient student of the truth. There was an even deeper way of rejoicing in the Lord, and that was by communion with God. They had not to do with a God who simply made a beautiful world and set it spinning and then withdrew Himself to an infinite distance from it—not with a God that spoke 1800 years ago and had since relapsed into a dead, impenetrable silence. He was a God who was still con- versible with men and held fellowship with His people. This fellowship with the living God was the greatest thing upon the earth. It was the only pleasure that never wore out and endured ander all circumstances. In the evening the Rev. A. C. Parker preached and MrPearse effectively sang a solo : " The Lord is my shepherd."

div.head: "The Devil In Bondage.",
div.p: "The Devil In Bondage.",

This formed the subject of an address which the Rev. J. F. Matthews delivered to a large congregation at Latchford Baptist Church on Sunday evening. Basing his remarks on Rev. xx. 1,2 and 3, he said we had yet. arrived at anything like a complete knowledge as to the class of literature which the book of Revelation belonged. The book was constructed with quite mechanical exactness, vision following vision with many correspondences and differences. In his text they had the figure of the devil chained and incarcerated in an abyss with the seal set upon him—a magnificent piece of imagery. First there was the complete confinement of evil, secondly its almost absolute annihilation, and thirdly its inherent power of re-asser- tion. Such interpretation whether accepted or not at least was true. The growing of the Kingdom of God narrowed the area over which evil reigned, and the ultimate triumph of goodness and truth was thereby assured, and the ordinary worker,especially the worker in hopeless causes should take heart from the fact that the Kingdom of God was marching on.

The Rey. Herbert Dunnico. An interesting article on the Rev. H. Dunnico's 1" call" to Kensington, written by the Rev. Alfred Barratt, of Warrington, appears in this week's issue of "The Christian Commonwealth.", The writer says : " Mr. Dunnico possesses many sterling qualifications, and has proved himself a hard worker, a fearless speaker, and a striver after right. Hence I do not think that he will face the future with misgivings. I believe that he has the confidence that the Lord who called him into the ministry has called him to Kensing- ton, and will not allow him to fail in that to which he is sent. As a minister he is second to none in Warring- ton, and is worthy of the honour conferred urn him by so large and important a cnurch, which I believe to be one of the leading churches in our denomination. His labours in Warrington will be looked upon ris unique in the history of the Baptist Church, for in four years he had done more to build up and strengthen it than any other minister before him. If Kensington knows its business it will rally round him and enable him to do for them what he has done for Warrington." On Sun- day evening the Rev. Herbert Dunnico will preach his farewell sermon in the Parr Hall. After the service a public presentation will be made to him by Alderman Bennett on behalf of a large number of subscribers.

Rey. Sidney Pitt and "The Duty of ' Happiness." • How People are prejudiced Against Christianity. At Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church on Sunday morning the Rev. Sidney Pitt preached on " The duty of happi- ness." He said they hearcl a great deal about the duty of self-denial, but not much about the duty of happiness. To some religious people happiness seemed to be a thing to be shunned and suspected rather than to be developed and cultivated. It was hardly an exaggera- tion to say of them that they were never happy unless they were miserable. People were often prejudiced against the religion of Christ by that foolish misunderstanding. Now what was the case? The Bible everywhere proclaimed the blessedness—that was,in our modern speech,the happiness of the righteoi Our Lord Himself in the one full and formal semi. that He preached set forth as the characteristics of 141 most faithful followers a whole string of beatitudes. —blessednesses and happiaess—showing those things to be happiness which the world had never counted as such before.
